editorials.title: Building consensus: On the 18th BRICS Summit, the New Delhi Declaration
editorials.passage:
Reaffirming the importance of reformed multilateralism in a world riven with unilateral actions by superpowers emerged as a binding theme of the 18th BRICS Summit and the New Delhi Declaration . The Summit’s success could be measured by three main parameters — the participation of members at the highest levels, the importance given to intra-BRICS trade cooperation mechanisms and the consensus achieved by Indian negotiators in forging a joint statement in a time of war. The government should be commended for ensuring that Iran and the UAE, two rivals in the West Asian conflict, used the occasion for their highest-level bilateral meeting since the war began. The New Delhi Declaration , which was issued despite scepticism about all the differences within the grouping, presented the BRICS as a formidable front in its 20th year. Among the BRICS members, the position of Saudi Arabia, which has yet to formally join the group, remains ambiguous, as Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud arrived after the main session where the joint statement was adopted on Saturday. For the other members, however, the consensus was clear on issues of global importance. The declaration made a call for the reform of the Security Council and support for a greater role for Brazil and India while recommending new initiatives for global governance. It condemned western sanctions and tariffs and resolved to improve intra-BRICS trade and transact more in local currencies. It also condemned unilateral wars, without criticising any member. While the statement omitted references to the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran , the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei , and of Iran’s retaliatory attacks on its neighbours, especially the UAE, it is understood that this was due to a last-moment compromise effected between the two countries so as to forge the agreed text. It also took an exceptionally strong position on Israel’s actions in Palestine and Lebanon.

India’s fourth BRICS chairship has given ballast to its reputation as a Global South balancer with easy access to both sides of a divided world, while delivering bilateral benefits. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s close attention to Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian would have gone some way in assuaging hurt feelings, when New Delhi appeared to be tilting towards the U.S. and Israel in the war. Mr. Modi’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping also afforded the two countries a chance to reaffirm their political will to normalise ties. And his meeting with important leaders from the ASEAN grouping and African nations paid much-needed attention to India’s ties with them. This BRICS Summit will be remembered for a moment of solidarity among countries that have many differences but are together in desiring a shift in traditional power equations to one more driven by their emerging economies.

editorials.title: A rising graph: On the doping culture in Indian sports
editorials.passage:
At least 13 doping positives in the run-up to the recent Commonwealth Games and the upcoming Asian Games have again put India in an embarrassing spotlight. For a country that has been notoriously leading the global doping charts for three consecutive years , the spate of positive results across disciplines including athletics, weightlifting, wrestling, wushu and judo, has not only brought shame but has also robbed India of some berths in these prestigious events. The dope-tainted names have forced authorities to pull them out of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games squad. More such names are expected to trickle out in the coming weeks. Lucrative cash incentives for Asian Games medallists are a major factor driving athletes and coaches to take shortcuts, risking their health and reputation, as well as the country’s pride. While the spike in dope-positive results ahead of major multi-sport events is not new, the jump this time is a cause for concern. The matter getting raised during the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) workshops in Delhi, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) downgrading India due to an extremely high risk of doping, and an international agency recently conducting surprise tests in Bhubaneswar and Bengaluru indicate the seriousness of the issue.

Even though National Sports Federations have been expressing concern, it cannot be said that they are strict to the core to curb the menace. Despite being seriously understaffed, the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA), which shoulders the primary anti-doping responsibility in India, has significantly increased the number of tests and raids based on intelligence gathering. But it needs to do more in a vast and populous country to discourage doping. Besides, NADA needs to get out of the government’s control to function truly independently in order to enhance its effectiveness. Proper implementation of the National Anti-Doping (Amendment) Act, 2025, to give more powers to NADA and its allied bodies, is another requirement. With dope testing becoming costlier and NADA needing more staff, the government can bolster the fight against doping by increasing the overall budget allocation, which was reduced in the current budget. The other challenge is to cut the supply line, as India has become a hub for the trade in banned substances sourced from different countries. An Indian serving a jail term in Kenya for illegally importing performance-enhancing drugs stands as proof of this. As India prepares for the 2030 Commonwealth Games and hopes to host the Olympics in the future, it needs to act resolutely to weed out a deep-rooted doping culture in Indian sports.

editorials.title: Language policy must reflect India's realities
editorials.passage: The Supreme Court’s query last month on whether English should be placed in the non-native language basket prompted the government to raise its guard last week. The question arose in the context of the CBSE’s directive to implement the three-language formula from this academic session. The Board’s May 15 circular made it mandatory for students to study three languages, at least two of them Indian. Those wanting to study a foreign language could take it as a third or additional fourth language. Relegating English to a third language was problematic, as was the short notice for implementing the order. When petitioners challenging the Board’s directive sought clarity from the Bench on English’s status last week, the CBSE opposed the request.As things stand, English is at the intersection of aspiration and national pride. Phasing it out by degrees could hardly have been the policy’s subtext, as that boat sailed long ago. While Macaulay’s colonial design to create a class of Anglicised intermediaries is undisputed, India has outgrown that purpose. Decades after Independence, English continues alongside Hindi for official purposes, having withstood attempts to displace it with Hindi, as resistance from the South was too strong to ignore. It has become a political bulwark against language imposition. It is embedded in the Constitution and higher judiciary, and remains central to litigation, science and technology. Proficiency in English opens doors to higher education and better job prospects. India’s software boom benefitted from its large pool of English-speaking talent..This is not an argument against the mother tongue. Proficiency in one’s first language can be crucial to a child’s cognitive development, while countries such as China and Japan have demonstrated that advanced economies can build strong education systems largely in their own languages. India’s linguistic diversity, however, makes its equation more complex. Regional pride is intertwined with the mother tongue, and there is no reason why Indians shouldn’t acquire more than one link language. The objective should be to expand access to knowledge, not restrict it by language.As Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said, “learning a language never goes to waste.” But if adding a third language increases student stress when competitive examinations are the focus, it may not be wise. The demand for policy change has to come from within society, not be imposed from the top, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said recently. editorials.title: Bigger BRICS test now: Turning Global South weight into influence
editorials.passage: The New Delhi Declaration, adopted after marathon negotiations, is a diplomatic win for India—and a test of BRICS’ evolving relevance. Despite differences over West Asia, members found common ground on restraint, civilian protection, sovereignty, diplomacy and nuclear safety. Importantly, the declaration reasserts BRICS’ ambition to reshape global governance, amplify the Global South and deepen cooperation across finance, trade, technology and development. That sets the stage for the harder task: delivering results.As BRICS expands and its economic and political weight grows, its credibility will increasingly depend on whether it can build institutions that deliver practical gains. The central question is whether an increasingly diverse grouping can turn collective weight into strategic capacity without demanding political uniformity from its members. That means moving faster on the architecture of a more resilient global economy. Cross-border payments, greater use of local currencies, development finance, investment platforms, insurance and financial safety nets are no longer abstract ideas. They are responses to a world of unilateral sanctions, tariff shocks, supply-chain disruptions and financial volatility. The challenge is to make these mechanisms interoperable, commercially viable and accessible enough to matter beyond government statements..Technology will be an acid test. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s warning about the weaponisation of technology and critical minerals points to a wider contest over who controls the infrastructure of the next economy. BRICS has an opportunity to cooperate on artificial intelligence, semiconductors, critical minerals, cybersecurity, digital public infrastructure and technology standards. But it must avoid creating competing technological silos. The same logic applies to health, food and energy security. The grouping has the scale to build stronger pandemic surveillance, medical supply chains, agricultural cooperation and mechanisms to cushion commodity and energy shocks. These are areas where cooperation can produce tangible benefits for citizens while giving the Global South a greater stake in BRICS.There is also a larger diplomatic task. BRICS cannot become effective by positioning itself merely against the West. Its influence will come from demonstrating that a more multipolar world can also be more stable, representative and capable of solving problems. India’s presidency secured the consensus it needed. Now comes the harder test: delivery at speed and scale. BRICS must move beyond declarations and convert the Global South’s collective weight into institutions, capabilities and tangible outcomes that can reshape global governance and strengthen its credibility..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | The cattle stake
editorials.passage: Kerala has just retired a job. Sosamma, the state’s last cattle-pound keeper, spent 30 years rounding up stray cattle and holding them until their owners reclaimed them. Unclaimed animals could be auctioned. The job became obsolete as animal-control systems changed, but the bovine mess is only worsening. Across India, abandoned cattle clog roads and highways, destroy crops and endanger lives; farmers and dairies discard male calves and dry cows when holding them becomes unviable. Gaushalas have hardly filled the breach. The Supreme Court recently flagged the danger again. Perhaps it’s time to bring back Sosamma—for all we know, she’s still the person properly qualified for a job we thought we didn’t need..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Growing up online
editorials.passage:
There was a time when a child’s social world was largely confined to the school, the neighbourhood playground and the family home. Today, much of that world fits inside a smartphone. Friendships are made and maintained through screens; entertainment arrives through endless scrolling; approval is measured in likes, shares and followers. Social media has become an important part of childhood and adolescence ~ but growing evidence suggests that its benefits come with significant psychological and social costs. The question is no longer whether children should use social media. 

It is how much, how early and under what safeguards they should use it. Psychologists across the globe are repeatedly warning that children and adolescents are particularly vulnerable to the pressures created by social media. The American Psychological Association (APA), in its health advisory on adolescent social-media use, does not argue that social media is inherently harmful. It recognises that online platforms can help young people maintain friendships, find communities, express themselves and obtain information. But it also stresses that the impact depends on the child's developmental stage, individual characteristics, the nature of online activity and the social environment surrounding the child. 

Significantly, APA states, “To reduce the risks of psychological harm, adolescents’ exposure to content on social media that depicts illegal or psychologically maladaptive behavior, including content that instructs or encourages youth to engage in health-risk behaviors, such as self-harm (e.g., cutting, suicide), harm to others, or those that encourage eating-disordered behavior (e.g., restrictive eating, purging, excessive exercise) should be minimized, reported, and removed; moreover, technology should not drive users to this content.” This distinction is crucial. A child watching an educational video for twenty minutes is not experiencing social media in the same way as a teenager spending three hours comparing appearance, popularity and lifestyle with carefully curated images of peers and influencers. 

Psychologists are especially concerned about social comparison. Children are still developing their identities and self-esteem. Constant exposure to images of apparently perfect bodies, beautiful homes, expensive possessions and exciting lifestyles can create the impression that everyone else is happier and more successful. The resulting gap between one's real life and the idealised online world can contribute to dissatisfaction, anxiety and low self-esteem. The problem is intensified by the design of many platforms. Notifications, recommendations, autoplay, short videos, likes and personalised feeds encourage users to remain engaged. For a developing brain, the immediate reward of a notification or positive reaction can be particularly powerful. 

Consequently, what begins as entertainment may gradually become habitual checking bordering on addiction. Another major concern is sleep. Children who take their phones to bed may continue scrolling long after they should be asleep. Notifications and the anticipation of new messages can keep the brain alert. Sleep deprivation, in turn, can affect concentration, memory, emotional regulation and academic performance. Thus, the damage may not arise from one particular post or video but from a lifestyle gradually reorganised around the smartphone. 

Yet it would be simplistic to declare social media the enemy. For many young people, especially those who feel isolated in their offline environments, online communities can provide friendship and emotional support. Children with particular interests can find communities that may not exist in their immediate surroundings. Social media can also promote creativity, civic engagement, cultural exchange and access to educational resources. The real concern, therefore, is unregulated and developmentally inappropriate use. Interestingly, that concern has increasingly moved from psychologists' offices into the courtrooms of many western countries, including the United States. 

For example, across the United States, thousands of lawsuits have been filed against major technology companies hosting social media platforms. The plaintiffs ~ including young people, parents, school districts and government authorities - allege that these platforms were designed in ways that encouraged compulsive use among children and adolescents and contributed to mental-health problems. Such courtroom battles are significant because they change the nature of the public conversation. The issue is no longer simply whether parents should tell children to put their phones away. 

Plaintiffs argue that responsibility should also fall upon companies whose business models depend upon sustained user engagement. The recent case of a technology giant paying $18 billion to settle lawsuits against its social media platforms and the harm it causes to children due to its addictive algorithms highlights that there is a growing awareness that social media platforms impact childhood in undesirable ways. These developments should not be misunderstood as a judicial declaration that social media causes every instance of depression, anxiety or self-harm. 

Human behaviour is extraordinarily complex. Mental health is influenced by family circumstances, genetics, poverty, academic pressure, peer relationships, trauma and many other factors. Scientific literature itself continues to debate causation, rather than merely association. Nevertheless, the lawsuits raise an important ethical question: Should social media platforms used extensively by children be designed primarily to maximise engagement, or should child wellbeing be the overriding principle? There is no single answer. Parents have an important role, but parental responsibility cannot carry the entire burden. 

Schools must teach digital literacy and help students recognise manipulation, misinformation, cyberbullying and unhealthy online behaviour. Psychologists can help children develop resilience, self-esteem and healthy patterns of technology use. Governments can establish age-appropriate safety standards and demand greater transparency from technology companies. Platforms themselves must build stronger privacy protections, effective age assurance, safer recommendation systems and meaningful parental controls. Perhaps the most sensible approach is neither a complete technological prohibition nor unrestricted access. 

Children need digital childhoods, but they also need real childhoods. Parents can begin with simple measures: keeping phones away during meals and homework, establishing screen-free periods before bedtime, turning off unnecessary notifications and discussing what children encounter online rather than simply policing their devices. Most importantly, adults should model the behaviour they expect from children. It is difficult to persuade a child to stop scrolling when every adult around them is doing precisely the same thing. The deeper lesson is that technology should serve childhood ~ not redefine it. 

A healthy childhood requires sleep, play, conversation, physical activity, face-to-face friendship, boredom, imagination and the freedom to make mistakes without an audience of thousands. The American social media debate ~ and the rapidly expanding courtroom battle against the technology giants ~ suggests that society is beginning to recognise a fundamental principle: children are not merely consumers. They are developing human beings who deserve an online environment designed with their wellbeing in mind. The challenge before parents, educators, psychologists, policymakers and technology companies is to ensure that the next generation grows up not as prisoners of the screen, but as masters of it.
   
(The writer is Assistant Professor in English, Pritilata Waddedar Mahavidyalaya, Nadia)

editorials.title: Economic siege may not defeat Iran
editorials.passage:
The United States’ new economic offensive against Iran may prove less decisive than Washington hopes. On August 24, the U.S. announced “Operation Economic Outcast”, imposing sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and ships across five sectors of Iran’s economy, from digital assets to shipping. The move seeks concessions without opening another military front. But can economic pressure achieve what military force and diplomacy have failed to deliver: a negotiated settlement of Iran’s nuclear programme? Under U.S. sanctions since 1979, Iran has built mechanisms to circumvent them. 

China is the crucial example. Despite American sanctions, it buys about 90 per cent of Iran’s crude exports, often at a discount of about $12 a barrel. Iran also relies on shadow banks and tankers. The damage is severe. The rial has weakened sharply since January. War damage to industry and refineries has contributed to fuel shortages, while inflation has reached 88 per cent. Iranian oil exports have fallen to a new low. Tehran has about 80 million barrels outside Hormuz, but sanctions make them difficult to monetise. Yet greater pressure may produce diminishing returns. Even if Washington imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese banks, Iran could use its own payment systems for oil transactions. Beijing has warned that the new sanctions threaten global growth and financial stability and has vowed to protect its legitimate interests. 

Washington will therefore be cautious about confronting China. Beijing’s restriction of rare-earth supplies last year demonstrated the potential cost of economic retaliation and was followed by President Donald Trump’s effort to improve relations with China. This exposes a contradiction in the American strategy. Washington wants to choke Iran’s economy without turning the confrontation into a wider contest with China. Aggressive pressure on Chinese institutions risks turning the crisis into another arena of U.S.-China rivalry. Iran believes the political clock favours it. Only 31 per cent of Americans, according to the latest survey, support continued military action against Iran. With the November midterm elections approaching, Trump has strong incentive to end the confrontation without appearing to concede defeat. Tehran understands this constraint. Keeping oil prices above $80 could increase pressure on the White House through higher energy costs. Hormuz provides Iran another source of leverage. 

Tehran has been close to an arrangement with Oman under which ships crossing the strait would pay tolls. This could increase pressure on Washington to enforce its embargo. But further U.S. attacks could damage American credibility without producing a decisive result. The central unresolved issue is nuclear. Iran’s nuclear programme and stockpile of fissile material remain substantially intact. When Trump launched “Epic Fury”, the expectation was that military pressure would weaken the Iranian regime and compel it to abandon its nuclear ambitions. When that failed, Washington offered sanctions relief and billions of dollars in investment, hoping Tehran would open Hormuz and give up its nuclear programme. That too failed. The economic offensive is now being used to achieve what force and inducements have not. The June MOU was significant. 

It offered Iran an end to U.S. opposition, protection for its proxies, sanctions relief, the unfreezing of oil revenues and $300 billion for reconstruction. In return, Iran would have had to eschew its nuclear programme and open Hormuz. President Masoud Pezeshkian wants Washington to return to the understanding. It demonstrates that a negotiated exit was possible. The difficulty is that Tehran now believes its bargaining position has improved. The Yemen front strengthens that perception. The Houthis have attacked Saudi ports, airports and refineries. 

Their objectives are economic and strategic: securing payments for Yemeni civil servants, lifting restrictions on flights and shipping, and obtaining a greater share of revenues from Yemen’s oil exports. Since 2014, they have controlled north-western Yemen, including Sana’a and much of the western coast. Geography and military adaptation favour the Houthis. They operate from defensible highlands and use mines, caves, bunkers and tunnels. They have access to fibre-optic drones that are difficult to jam. In 2025, they shot down seven U.S. Reaper drones and nearly hit American fighter aircraft. Last month, they reportedly brought down a Turkish-made Bayraktar drone operated by Saudi forces and have begun developing their own drones. 

Pressure on Iran can now reverberate across both the Gulf and Red Sea. Iran’s leadership adds another complication. The emerging establishment differs from the model associated with Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who balanced competing interests by alternating between reformists and hardliners. The new generation of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders appears more action-oriented, security-focused and results-driven. Mohsen Rezaei is the new national security adviser, while Ahmed Vahidi and Hossein Taeb represent the harder security establishment. 

Seven senior leaders are consolidating power, while Mojtaba Khamenei has remained absent from public life. The new leadership therefore appears more uncompromising than its predecessor, although its longer-term direction remains uncertain. For Washington, the blockade may be less a route to victory than an attempt to avoid another war. Iran may still negotiate, but its new leadership is unlikely to accept coercion without demanding substantial financial and strategic compensation. The MOU offers a possible exit because it contained major economic incentives. Washington must use that opening without appearing to reward resistance. 

For India, the implications are immediate. A prolonged confrontation threatens oil prices, shipping through Hormuz and maritime commerce through the Red Sea. India’s energy security and trade are therefore vulnerable to developments beyond its control. China’s continuing purchase of Iranian oil could make the crisis another arena of U.S.-China competition, complicating India’s calculations. Economic coercion can weaken Iran without resolving the nuclear question. 

Decades of sanctions have forced Tehran to develop alternative financial and trading channels, while China provides an important economic outlet. Military pressure has not eliminated Iran’s strategic capabilities, and diplomacy has yet to bridge the fundamental dispute. For India, therefore, the significance of the U.S. economic siege lies not simply in whether Washington can impose greater pain on Tehran, but in whether it can convert that pressure into a political settlement without turning the Gulf, Hormuz and the Red Sea into a wider strategic confrontation. 

The writer, a retired Brigadier of the Indian Army, is an analyston geopolitics, international and defence affairs.

editorials.title: Orangutan Trail
editorials.passage:
Five baby orangutans turning up in an Odisha forest should not be treated as an oddity of the animal kingdom. It is a warning about the reach of international wildlife trafficking and, potentially, about India’s place in that illicit trade. The animals could not have reached Balasore naturally. They belong to rainforests thousands of kilometres away in Indonesia and Malaysia. Their discovery together, without adults, points overwhelmingly towards human transportation. Their apparent familiarity with people makes the possibility of captivity before abandonment even harder to dismiss. What makes the case significant is the emerging Indonesian connection. 

Indonesia has entered discussions with Indian authorities and sought the return of the animals if their Indonesian origin is established. Preliminary assessment has reportedly raised the possibility that they are Sumatran orangutans, although DNA testing will be necessary to establish their provenance conclusively. That distinction matters. It would be premature to declare that Indonesia is the source of this particular consignment, still less to identify those responsible. But the possibility deserves serious investigation because it could reveal something considerably larger than an isolated smuggling episode. Indian investigators are examining whether the animals travelled by road and whether Odisha was a transit point rather than their intended destination. 

The location near the West Bengal border is important. If the animals entered India through the Northeast or another international route and were subsequently moved through West Bengal and Odisha, the case could expose a trafficking corridor that has so far remained largely invisible. There is also a disturbing economic logic behind such trafficking. Orangutans are critically endangered, difficult to obtain legally and highly desirable to collectors of exotic animals. Their rarity increases their value precisely because their capture is illegal. The five infants therefore represent not merely wildlife but commodities in an international black market. 

India has strong wildlife-protection legislation and agencies tasked with combating wildlife crime. Yet legislation is only as effective as the intelligence, border surveillance, forensic capacity and international cooperation behind it. A trafficking network capable of moving five infant creatures across national borders is unlikely to depend on improvisation alone. It requires transport, intermediaries, money and buyers. That is why the investigation should not end with identifying whoever abandoned the animals in Balasore. Authorities should reconstruct the entire journey: where the orangutans originated, how they entered India, who transported them, who financed the movement and where they were supposed to go. 

The Indonesian request for repatriation adds an important diplomatic dimension. India and Indonesia have close strategic relations, but wildlife crime offers a different kind of test of bilateral cooperation. If these animals are proved to have originated in Indonesia, their return should become part of a wider effort to dismantle the network that removed them from their natural habitat. The tracing of the animals has given Indian authorities something more valuable than five rescued animals: a possible trail. The real test is whether they follow it all the way to its source ~ and its intended destination.

editorials.title: Pentagon Purge
editorials.passage:
The most consequential question raised by the turmoil at the Pentagon is not whether Pete Hegseth has the authority to remove senior military officers. A civilian secretary of defence ~ or war ~ must have that authority. The question is what happens when personnel changes become a mechanism for enforcing conformity rather than implementing policy. Since assuming his position, Hegseth has removed or sidelined an extraordinary number of senior officers. 

The latest departures include Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who had been closely involved in an ambitious programme to reshape the Army, Gen. Randy George, the Army’s chief of staff, and Gen. Chris Donahue, another senior commander. The cumulative effect is more important than any individual dismissal: a substantial part of the Army’s senior leadership has been disrupted while America is engaged in active conflict. There is a legitimate argument behind Hegseth’s transformation agenda. The American military has accumulated expensive legacy systems, cumbersome procurement procedures and layers of bureaucracy. Ukraine has demonstrated how quickly drones, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare and commercially available technology can alter warfare. 

The Pentagon cannot respond to those changes by protecting every existing institution and weapon system. Yet reform becomes hazardous when professional disagreement is treated as disloyalty. The irony is that Driscoll and George were themselves pursuing significant transformation. The Army had been experimenting with new approaches to drones and autonomous systems and studying lessons from Ukraine. Their removal therefore cannot simply be explained as the triumph of reform over an entrenched military establishment. It also reflects a struggle over who defines reform, and which professional judgments are permitted to influence it. 

That distinction matters because military organisations depend on candour. Generals are not supposed to be independent political actors, but neither are they political appointees. Their value to civilian leaders lies partly in their willingness to explain operational realities that may be inconvenient or unpopular. If officers come to believe that disagreeing with the secretary can end their careers, the resulting institution may become more obedient but less useful. Senior commanders can learn to anticipate what political leaders want to hear. That is a particularly dangerous form of institutional decay because it is largely invisible until a serious decision goes wrong. The timing makes the experiment riskier still. 

The United States is fighting Iran while confronting Russia, China and the rapidly changing character of warfare. The Pentagon simultaneously needs continuity in command and the freedom to challenge assumptions. Hegseth may ultimately succeed in making the military leaner, more technologically capable and less bureaucratic. His critics may also be wrong about the consequences of his personnel decisions. But reform cannot be judged solely by how decisively a secretary imposes it. 

The real test is whether the reformed institution becomes better at thinking, adapting and telling uncomfortable truths. A powerful secretary can replace generals. He cannot quickly replace the institutional knowledge those generals accumulated. And that is the gamble now being taken at the Pentagon.

editorials.title: History lessons
editorials.passage:
With the death of Sumit Sarkar in Delhi at the age of 87 on August 13, an era in the writing of Indian history closed quietly. Sarkar was the last surviving member of a remarkable cohort of Bengali historians — Ranajit Guha, Tapan Raychaudhuri, Ashin Das Gupta, Sabyasachi Bhattacharya and Sarkar himself. Five historians of very different temperaments and specialisations who reshaped how modern India understands its past. Their deaths, spread across a little less than three decades, mark the passing of a mode of inquiry disciplined by archives, argument, and doubt, precisely at the moment when it is under siege from a louder, faster, and far less scrupulous way of recounting the past.

This quintet by no means exhausts the stalwarts among historians from contemporary Bengal (I am thinking of Amales Tripathi, Binay Bhushan Chaudhuri and Kirti Narayan Chaudhuri, among others) or the rest of India (thankfully, Irfan Habib and Romila Thapar are still practising their craft). It is a personal choice, weighing impact on Indian and global historiography alongside influence on my own formation as a student, researcher, and teacher of history. I had the privilege of knowing each of them, though my interaction with Guha was brief and, among the five, only Das Gupta taught me in a few special classes at the University of Calcutta. But I learnt from reading their works that their disagreements — sometimes fundamental — about class, nationalism, culture, colonial modernity, and the historian’s craft were themselves part of their legacy. They demonstrated that scholarly traditions are built not by enforcing unanimity but by making disagreement answerable to evidence.

Ranajit Guha, who taught at various institutions in Calcutta before moving to Manchester and Sussex and then to Canberra, died in Vienna in 2023, just weeks short of his 100th birthday. His early work, A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963), dissected the ideological assumptions behind the Permanent Settlement of 1793 with a precision that unsettled colonial economic history. But it was as founder of the Subaltern Studies Collective that Guha changed the field permanently. His insistence, in Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983), that peasant rebellions had their own coherent political grammar — rather than being inarticulate outbursts awaiting elite leadership to become ‘real’ politics — forced Indian historiography to reckon with agency from below. History written only from the vantage of the State and its elites was, he insisted, not history at all but the administration’s self-portrait.

Tapan Raychaudhuri — he taught at Calcutta University, the Delhi School of Economics and Oxford, and died in 2014 — offered something like a counterweight. A meticulous economic historian, his Bengal Under Akbar and Jahangir (1953) remains a foundational study of Mughal-era social history, and his editorship of the Cambridge Economic History of India shaped a generation’s understanding of colonial economic structures. But Europe Reconsidered (1988) and Perceptions, Emotions, Sensibilities (1999) perhaps best display his subtlety, demonstrating that 19th-century Bengali responses to Europe — far from being simple imitation or resistance — were acts of selective appropriation, fascination, and judgement. His classic Bengali memoir, Bangalnama (2007), alive with wit and self-irony, reminded us that historical intelligence includes the ability to examine one’s own world without solemnity.

Ashin Das Gupta taught at Presidency College and Visva-Bharati and died of a critical illness in 1998. He made the Indian Ocean a densely inhabited historical arena long before ‘oceanic history’ became fashionable. Working through Dutch and other European company records, he reconstructed — in Malabar in Asian Trade (1967, developing out of his Cambridge PhD thesis) and Indian Merchants and the Decline of Surat (1979) — the teeming worlds of merchants, brokers, shipowners, financiers, port communities, and fragile networks of trust. His merchants were neither faceless agents of an abstract market nor passive casualties of European expansion but actors navigating unstable sovereignties and making choices under pressure. My favourite is the portrait of Mulla Abdul Ghafur in the Surat book: a masterclass in reading a whole economy through one life — an early-18th-century Bohra merchant of immense wealth but no political ambition and no institution to outlast him whose vanished fortune became the epitaph of Surat itself.

Sabyasachi Bhattacharya, who taught briefly at Jadavpur before a long career at Jawaharlal Nehru University and died in 2019, showcased an equally striking range. His first book, The Financial Foundations of the British Raj (1971), exposed imperial power through budgets, revenue, and the reconstruction of public finance after 1857. He went on to intervene in labour history, education, archives, nationalism, and the intellectual worlds of Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore. My personal favourites are his slender biography of the song, “ Vande Mataram ” — so very apposite for today’s times — and his wonderful introduction to the utterly compelling The Mahatma and the Poet (1997), on the Tagore-Gandhi debates. As teacher, institution-builder, and leader of professional bodies, he understood that scholarship depends upon institutions: archives preserved, journals sustained, young researchers trained, disagreement protected.

Sumit Sarkar, who taught for some time at the Universities of Calcutta and Burdwan and then for three decades at Delhi University, connected many of these concerns with exceptional force. The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal (1973) remains exemplary because it neither canonised nationalism nor underplayed its significance, examining leadership and mass participation, economic grievance and cultural symbolism, mobilisation and its limits. Modern India , 1885-1947 (1983) introduced generations to a history at once synoptic and alert to workers, peasants, women, caste and communal conflict. As an early participant in the Subaltern Studies project, Sarkar helped enlarge the historian’s field of vision; as a later critic, he warned — especially in Writing Social History (1997) — against abandoning material histories for an overly textualised celebration of ‘community’ or ‘fragments’. His willingness to revise his affiliations without relinquishing intellectual commitments was itself a lesson in scholarly integrity. So was his consistent public opposition to the communal rewriting of India’s past.

All five were born in the 1920s and 1930s, and all studied at Presidency College, the first two in late-colonial India and through Independence and Partition, and the remaining three in the 1950s. Three took their doctorates at the University of Calcutta — Raychaudhuri (before a second DPhil at Oxford), Bhattacharya, and Sarkar — a mark of that university’s research strength in those years. All five wrote in Bengali as well, showcasing the finest standards of bilingual scholarship. It seems extraordinary that from Raychaudhuri’s first book in 1953 down to Sarkar’s death a month ago, their works have been beacons of scholarship for more than 70 years.

These historians treated historical truth as provisional, yet never arbitrary. Any of their interpretations could be challenged but only with evidence, context, and argument. Each offered a discipline of attention that today’s ‘WhatsApp history’ — which replaces citation with repetition, chronology with grievance, and explanation with a fable of immaculate heroes and congenital traitors — threatens to dissolve. As we see each day, the purpose of this spurious history is to supply instant ancestry to present identities and instant legitimacy to present power. For today’s young scholars, the lesson is not to match that speed but to refuse its terms — learning the languages, entering the archives, reading evidence fairly, arguing across camps, and revising when the argument demands it. Unlike the forwarded message, real history takes a lifetime of patience — and a constant, critical doubt for all certainties. Ranajit Guha dedicated A Rule of Property for Bengal “To my teacher Professor Sushobhan Sarkar/ who stoked so many of my first doubts.” In this age of WhatsApp history’s spurious and pernicious certitudes, those doubts are the most important legacy these five historians leave us.

Jayanta Sengupta is Professor, SHSS, TCG CREST, Calcutta

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: The pitfalls of 'whimsymaxxing’, a new trend in the West
editorials.passage:
Sir — There was a time when being whimsical meant being unusual, playful, and imaginative. Now, apparently, it means being wasteful. The West has discovered a new trend, ‘whimsymaxxing’, which involves taking single-use plastic items and dressing up or decorating with it. The internet is flooded with images and tutorials of influencers hot-glueing plastic beads onto mirrors and bedazzling their foreheads with shattered plastic forks. But what happens to these ‘masterpieces’ after the cameras are turned off? They end up in the landfill. Perhaps capitalism’s biggest achievement is convincing people that overconsumption is somehow creative.

Sir — When the United States of America suffered a terrorist attack on September 11, 2001, it reshaped the global security architecture (“25 years after 9/11, nation gathers to grieve”, Sept 12). The attacks transformed terrorism from background noise into an existential dread for many. Orchestrated by Al Qaida, 9/11 rewrote the public understanding of terrorism and reset national security assessments. The war on terror may have weakened terrorist networks but it has failed to eliminate the threat completely.

Sir — The 25th anniversary of 9/11 must compel the US to consider what its response to that tragedy did to the world and to the country itself. From Vietnam to Iraq and Afghanistan, American power has repeatedly crossed borders in the name of security and freedom, leaving immense human costs in its wake (“Terror’s long shadow”, Sept 12). The invasion of Iraq, in particular, exposed the dangers of power unconstrained by truth or accountability.

Sir — The terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, remain a stark reminder that the effects of terrorism extend far beyond the immediate and tragic loss of lives. A quarter of a century later, the true measure of our resilience lies in our ability to prevent fear from hardening into inherited prejudice, especially among younger generations.

Brij Bhushan Goyal, Ludhiana

Sir — The report, “Mis­sion: ‘Punish’ teachers” (Sept 11), laid bare an alar­ming threat to academic freedom. The passage of the West Bengal Universities and Colleges (Administration and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 followed by the chief minister’s suggestion that dissatisfied teachers could quit, shows how forced transfers may be weaponised to discipline educators. Turning the acronym JUTA — it stands for the Jadavpur University Teachers’ Association — into a derogatory pun to mock respected academics displays contempt for the community and appears to be intended to break the faculty’s collective spirit. It was distasteful and revealed a lack of education.

Sir — The new teachers’ transfer bill allows experienced faculty members to be transferred to newer universities. The government claims that the measure will help transform these institutions into centres of excellence. But concerns remain that some of its provisions are vulnerable to misuse and could undermine the autonomy of institutions.

Sir — Many pressing matters in West Bengal demand the State’s immediate attention. Instead, the chief minister’s priority appears to be settling scores with political rivals. The government’s misplaced priorities could not be more glaring.

A.G. Rajmohan, Andhra Pradesh

Sir — Ishan Kishan, the captain of East Zone, deserves to be praised for leading from the front with a magnificent 270 runs against South Zone at Chepauk in the Duleep Trophy final. He followed it with 80 runs in the second innings, taking his match tally to 350 runs. East Zone’s imposing total of 708 gave the side a 372-run first-innings lead and ultimately secured the trophy for the team even though the match ended in a draw.

Sir — The Board of Control for Cricket in India should encourage its state associations to invite local schoolchildren to domestic fixtures. Such a step would benefit the future of Indian cricket. Giving students an opportunity to watch prominent cricketers compete in high-level tournaments, such as the Duleep Trophy final in Chennai, could inspire budding players and cultivate lasting interest among potential spectators.

M.R. Jayanthi, Coimbatore

Sir — It is heartening to see East Zone claim the Duleep Trophy after a 13-year wait, having last secured the title in the 2012-13 season. The triumph reflects the progress cricket has made in eastern India. Leading decisively from the front, Ishan Kishan was deservedly named Player of the Match. His outstanding contribution in both innings further strengthens his credentials in the red-ball format.

editorials.title: Green data
editorials.passage:
India runs a vast groundwater monitoring network. The Central Ground Water Board has tracked water levels through nearly 23,000 wells four times a year since 1969. Yet, under the National Hydrology Project, only about 5,260 of roughly 25,000 stations will receive Digital Water Level Recorders with telemetry. Most wells are still read by hand. A network measuring depleting aquifers retains a cadence designed before computers entered government offices.

This is the story of India’s environmental governance. The country has built real-time systems for tax collection, welfare transfers and digital payments. UPI processed 23.2 billion transactions in May 2026, according to data from the National Payments Corporation of India. Environmental governance has had no equivalent push. India has the technical capacity for real-time environmental measurement, but has not prioritised it.

Groundwater is the mild version because it is at least measured. For almost a decade, India’s national wetland map relied on 2006-07 satellite imagery, mapped at 1:50,000 scale. A newer atlas, based on 2017-18 imagery, arrived in 2022, estimating 15.98 million hectares. A 2024 refinement, using 2018-19 imagery, revised this to 16.89 million hectares. The decade-long gap, without a statutory survey cycle, is the problem. Wetlands regulate floods, recharge aquifers and support migratory birds, yet India has no schedule for tracking change.

Forests turn speed into a question of trust. Between 2014 and 2024, India diverted over 1.73 lakh hectares of forest land for non-forest use, according to the environment ministry. Each diversion should trigger compensatory afforestation, the planting of an equivalent or larger area elsewhere, tracked through the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority and Parivesh, its digital clearance portal. Yet, a 2023 Comptroller and Auditor General audit of South Sagar forest division, in Madhya Pradesh, found that 1,66,685 saplings were recorded as planted at Mun­deri and Singpur. Physical verification found only 1,20,321; 46,364 were unaccounted for. The record said one thing, the ground another, until an auditor visited years later.

The pattern recurs across pollution monitoring, biodiversity records and climate-adaptation spending. India has invested in CGWB’s wells, satellite-based wetland surveys, Parivesh and IN-GRES, a groundwater-assessment platform built with IIT Hyderabad. It has not invested equally in fixed refresh schedules or independent verification. The plumbing exists but nobody has been told to turn the taps on.

Environmental decisions carry economic and diplomatic weight. Forest clearances unlock projects worth thousands of crores. Groundwater depletion across Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan threatens food security across the Indo-Gangetic belt. At COP30, in Belem, India pressed developed countries for faster, larger adaptation finance. Its case would carry more weight if it could show, nearly in real time, how much forest remains, how fast aquifers are falling and whether afforestation targets exist on the ground rather than on forms.

The fix needs no new ministry or grand mission. The environment and Jal Shakti ministries should do for environmental data what the finance ministry did for payments: set a public deadline for fitting every CGWB well with telemetry; refresh the wetland inventory every five years; and open CAMPA’s plantation records to a public audit trail comparable to UPI’s. India became a global leader in digital governance by treating data infrastructure as essential. Its environment ministry must make the same decision, with a named timeline and owner. A country cannot govern what it refuses to measure.

editorials.title: Options open: Editorial on New Delhi's balancing act in a turbulent world
editorials.passage:
Amidst a series of meetings that Prime Minister Narendra Modi held over two days with visiting world leaders on the margins of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, three stood out. Mr Modi’s meetings with the leaders of China, Russia and Iran were significant not only for their substance but also the messages that they sent to a world in greater churn than at any point since the end of the Cold War. The wars waged on Iran and on Ukraine by the United States of America and Russia, respectively, have upended the global economy, disrupting supply chains and raising the costs of food and fertilisers, crude and consumer goods alike. China, the US’s principal rival, is lock­ed in maritime and territorial disputes with most of its neighbours, including India. Against this backdrop, Mr Modi’s meetings with the leaders of China, Russia and Iran have demonstrated that India remains among the world’s few countries that can enjoy close relations with the West while building meaningful partnerships with the nations that the West, especially the US, views with suspicion.

The most important message Mr Modi’s meetings sent, though, was to the countries whose leaders he met. The meetings show an acknowledgement on India’s part that each of these three relationships is vital for New Delhi’s own strategic calculus. Mr Modi may nudge the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, towards negotiations with Ukraine but New Delhi knows it needs the stability of Russian military and energy support as a counterbalance to the chaotic politics of the US and Europe. China may be India’s most significant strategic challenge but it is also the biggest source of Indian imports and is a neighbour New Delhi cannot wish away. The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, visited India after seven years, underscoring that Beijing, too, is willing to manage the relationship with India in a way that works for both nations without committing them to an embrace. This was Mr Modi’s second meeting with the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in two weeks — they also met on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek where Mr Modi also met Mr Putin. It was a signal that even amid its tightening ties with the US, Israel and Gulf Arab states, New Delhi is not willing to give up on relations with Tehran. In a fluid world, keeping options open is smart foreign policy.

editorials.title: Stubborn stain: Editorial on Bengal's failure to curb child marriage
editorials.passage:
The chief minister of West Bengal, Suvendu Adhikari, revealed that the state has recorded the highest number of child marriages and underage pregnancies in the country. According to a report prepared by the state health department, nearly 60,000 institutional deliveries by underage girls were reported between January 1 and June 30 this year. Murshidabad recorded the highest figure among districts with around 13,000 such childbirths, followed by South 24 Parganas with 4,178 cases. This is not an aberration. Data from the Sample Registration System released in 2025 revealed something similar: West Bengal led the nation with 6.3% of all current marriages involving girls under 18 — nearly triple the national average of 2.1%. Moreover, the National Family and Health Survey 5, conducted between 2019 and 2021, found that 41.6% of women aged between 20-24 in Bengal were married before the legally permissible age of 18. The intersection of geography and socio-economic realities of the districts suffering the malaise are revealing. A 2024 study identified Murshidabad, Birbhum, East and West Midnapore as districts where the situation was particularly concerning. It found significant associations between child marriage and education, place of residence and household wealth. The implications of this malpractice are serious. Early marriage and pregnancy lead to adolescent mothers facing greater health risks, losses in schooling years and employment opportunities, as well as restricted economic agency.

Mr Adhikari has blamed the rising cases of underage marriage on the “apathy” of the erstwhile Trinamool Congress dispensation, which, he alleged, failed to share data with the Centre. The previous government’s reliance on welfare schemes alone to tackle the social evil is worth questioning. Kanyashree was conceived to keep girls in school and delay marriage; yet evidence continues to show that cash incentives cannot, by themselves, overturn entrenched social norms. But a blame game is hardly the best response to an embedded social evil. The chief minister’s emphasis seems to be on a slew of punitive measures as a deterrent. The proposed punitive measures, including action under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 as well as penalties for husbands, families and those facilitating marriages, are necessary. But punishment cannot be the principal strategy. Sustained intervention in the form of sensitisation, economic rehabilitation and, most importantly, the spread of education along with targeted doles is necessary.

editorials.title: A tale of two systems
editorials.passage:
Another BRICS summit is over. China with its trade surpluses was clearly the overwhelming big daddy. It accounts for over 60 per cent of intra-BRICS trade and investment. Russia with its oil ran a close second. India trailed far behind with nine tail-enders.

Many people in India are full of admiration for China’s economic success, like they were for Pakistan in the 1980s. But Pakistan went phut because it didn’t have the political systems and institutions to sustain growth. China has the same problem. From 1950 to 1980 we admired and copied the USSR which also went phut in 1990.

That’s why I always ask people who admire China if they would like to swap our political system and institutions with China’s. No answer is forthcoming.

But let’s leave aside the politics and sociology and examine the India-China comparisons from a purely economic lens. The starting point has to be the acknowledgement that neoclassical economics is founded on the idea of political liberties, which China doesn’t permit. But we have a surfeit of these liberties.

Chinese GDP, meanwhile, is $20 trillion. Ours is not even five. So the question has to be whether the absence of such liberties facilitates rapid growth in industrial output.

In China it does, but in the USSR it didn’t. The West also didn’t have full political liberties — of the sort we have had since 1950 — till about 50 years ago. You can check this out.

There can be no doubt whatsoever that political liberties and rapid economic growth are inversely related. When you expand one, the other contracts. The more you have of the former the slower will the latter be. Look at East Asia after 1990.

There are no exceptions to this rule because growth depends on giving primacy to capital. Strange as it may sound, this is Marx 101. And it’s not just China, all the ‘Asian Tigers’ were like that. This has been said by several Nobel winning economists as well.

Unconstrained optimisation means capital flows into China and flows out of India. Period. Our emphasis on liberties means capital gets short shrift.

All our laws favour labour because we are a rights-based society. And when we try to correct the imbalance, as in 1991 or 2006 or 2019, there is protest. Just look at the number of trades unions and NGOs jumping up and down all the time and laying siege to the Supreme Court.

It must be asked why liberals object to a politically hard state, which is what we need for ever increasing investment and industrial output. You can’t have one without the other. It doesn’t work like that.

Also, when was the last time anyone compared Indian agricultural performance with China’s? India achieved food self-sufficiency in the 1970s, so much so that the massive drought of 1979 went unnoticed by the world. China is nowhere near it.

In fact, food is one of China’s biggest vulnerabilities alongside energy. It has enough of neither. All the world has to do is to reduce food and energy exports to China by 10 or 15 per cent and we will see how the paper tiger roars. India is quite safe that way.

We also have absolutely no idea of the efficiency of its capital use. The fact that the government’s first priority is employment, Chinese industry is hugely subsidised. That has created what economists call a moral hazard problem: there is very little incentive to save on capital. Few people realise it but China has made the same mistakes as the old Soviet Union where efficiency is concerned.

The point I am making is that when you compare two entirely different systems of governance you shouldn’t just look at one part and draw large conclusions. The correct questions to ask must be about systemic stability: which countries have stable systems and which are resting on a pin?

If Chinese political stability is ensured by massive force and widespread denial of political rights, Indian economic stability is ensured by suppressing economic freedoms. Which is preferable?

What would happen if China allowed even a fraction of Indian political rights and India allowed a small degree of Chinese economic freedom? Neither is going to happen.

China has a lot of hugely subsidised economic competition. We have a lot of hugely subsidised political competition. You can choose between them.

That’s why we should stop admiring what we don’t have and start boasting about what we do and keep expanding those things. China has the economic brawn but not the political brain. And that is going to be its biggest long term liability.

Published on September 14, 2026

editorials.title: NSE has priced everything except itself
editorials.passage:
For three decades, the National Stock Exchange (NSE) has priced everything India owns except itself. That is about to change. The exchange filed its draft red herring prospectus on June 17, 2026, for 148.9 million shares, close to six per cent of paid-up capital. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has since issued its observation letter. Before a traded price begins to summarise the exchange, its record and unfinished agenda deserve an audit.

The record begins with an index. NSE created the Nifty and made it the benchmark for Indian equity risk. Its pull took a slice of India’s price discovery offshore, to a Singapore Exchange contract. The answer was construction, not a ban. Since NSE International Exchange began full operations at Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City) on July 3, 2023, the GIFT Nifty contract has recorded more than 69.56 million contracts and $3.21 trillion in turnover.

Next came operational credibility. In the mid-1990s, screen-based trading across a national network, straight-through settlement and a clearing corporation standing between every buyer and seller were rare. That is why foreign portfolio investors treated India as a destination, not an experiment. Registered investors rose from 30.87 million in March 2020 to 129.1 million in March 2026. The growth is no longer confined to metropolitan areas: Uttar Pradesh led new registrations in 2024-25, adding 29.5 lakh investors. The same instinct built institutions. In 1996, the exchange set up the National Securities Depository Ltd along with the Industrial Development Bank of India and the Specified Undertaking of the Unit Trust of India. The depository was listed last year, with NSE among its selling shareholders. The pattern extended to NSE Indices, NSE Data and Analytics, NSE Clearing, and the exchange and clearing corporation at GIFT City. Some capabilities were built and then handed over: acting on the Mahalingam Committee’s recommendations, the exchange exited its technology and skilling businesses in early 2025. Letting go of what specialists can run better says as much as the balance sheet.

That balance sheet is unusual. Revenue from operations was ₹16,601 crore in FY26, with profit of ₹10,302 crore, both easing after SEBI’s derivative measures. Operating margins are near 76 per cent, net debt is zero, and the treasury book stands at about ₹64,771 crore. Roughly 51.2 per cent of global equity derivative contracts pass through the exchange, a position held for seven consecutive years, along with about 93 per cent of cash equity turnover.

What does listing add to an institution that is already considered a deemed listed entity, with disclosures, board, and conflict norms equal to or better than those of a listed company? The regulations remain largely the same; however, their enforcement varies significantly. Since the exchange lacks a promoter and the Life Insurance Corporation of India holds the largest stake at 10.72 per cent, ownership is widely spread; the listing will make the market the key oversight mechanism.

The open agenda deserves equal attention. Listed companies have a combined market value of ₹411 trillion across nearly 3,000 firms, while the corporate bond market is a fraction of that and municipal debt is barely present. Commodity derivatives remain thin in an economy that lives off agriculture and now leans on manufacturing. The Emerge platform for smaller firms was worth ₹1.8 trillion in March 2025. Retail’s share of market value reached a 22-year high of 18.75 per cent in the second quarter of 2025-26, but retail money still prefers short-dated derivatives to ownership. Each gap is a multi-year commitment that a listed company must defend every quarter.

The offer structure is often misread. It is only an offer for sale, so the money goes to the selling shareholders and not to the exchange. The Life Insurance Corporation, the State Bank of India, other banks and development finance institutions have held the stake for decades at close to original cost. Listing turns a locked strategic holding into liquid capital when the primary market needs it. The timing is a test in itself. With a heavy pipeline lined up for the coming quarters, an issue of this size will measure domestic institutional and household demand better than any survey.

For regulators, the listing carries forward what corporatisation and demutualisation began. For investors, it offers an asset whose returns follow the market’s activity rather than its direction. For policymakers, the sharper question is not what the exchange has built, but which of the remaining gaps it will now be pressed to close, when 129 million investors can also be its shareholders and its performance is priced every day.

The writer is Partner, MCQube

Published on September 14, 2026

editorials.title: Below the Line
editorials.passage:
One bus, one dinner — and one notable absence. Chinese President Xi Jinping gave Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s gala dinner a miss, even as Russian President Vladimir Putin and other BRICS leaders joined the host for the evening reception. Union ministers and chief ministers of several States were also present. In a touch of unusual choreography, the ministers and chief ministers attending the dinner arrived at the venue in a single bus from Parliament, turning the journey itself into a small spectacle of the summit.

BRICS diplomacy acquired a distinctly musical note in Delhi on Saturday, with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, in the capital for the summit, being seen singing Kishore Kumar’s iconic “ Khwab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat ” from the 1965 film Teen Deviyan . The unexpected rendition of the Bollywood classic offered a lighter moment amid the high-powered diplomacy surrounding the summit.

While the main stage buzzed with AI and tokenisation, much of the action at Global Fintech Fest was happening off it. Day one saw SEBI Chairman and IOSCO’s top brass in not one but two closed-door meetings, with no livestream and little detail on what was discussed. Elsewhere, State Bank of India Chairman CS Setty was spotted working the crowd, despite not being on the public agenda for the day. Add another dozen or so such sessions across three long days, including those involving FATF and RBI, and even a private GIFT City interaction with the Finance Minister, and it seemed this year’s real fintech conversations were happening behind closed doors. Meanwhile, Sarvam AI set itself apart by livestreaming its entire ‘closed-door’ meeting but kept the media present at the venue out of the hall.

At NSE’s pre-IPO press meet, perspective, reporters were reminded, comes with time. NSE MD and CEO Ashishkumar Chauhan, responding to concerns over how the industry would navigate a tougher regulatory environment, suggested that reporters had not “tracked exchanges as a business long enough” to understand market cycles. Chauhan also made a rare switch to Gujarati when answering one query for the relevant audience.

Questions on the lower price band and offer size were shrugged off to the investment bankers, none of whom were part of the answering panel, despite all 20 being present in the room. Invitations for the press meet went out only the previous midnight, while foreign media were conspicuously left out.

South African president Cyril Ramaphosa made a pitch to Indian corporates to invest in the country. While most of Ramaphosa’s address at a CII organised roundtable focused on reforms and improved credit rating, he ended it on a lighter note that drew laughter. “Yesterday I went to the BRICS business forum I had a little bit of cold which I usually develop with too much air conditioning. So my sense of smell was little bit reduced,” the president said. “This morning I woke up a lot better. As I entered this room and because my sense of smell has improved greatly I could smell money. So meeting you here I have a greater sense that I am in the presence of people with money. So I want you to come and invest in South Africa,” he remarked.

Published on September 14, 2026

editorials.title: The manufacturing fabric
editorials.passage: By Ashok Gulati & Sulakshana Rao In his Independence Day address last month, Prime Minister Narendra Modi placed “manufacturing power” as the first among the seven streams (saptadhara) that will help India achieve the vision of Viksit Bharat. He also said that in that effort the potential of India’s youth would be fully harnessed. The pertinent question is which manufacturing sector can actually deliver jobs at the scale India needs. ALSO READSecuring our skies on our terms Our research at ICRIER points to textiles and apparel (T&A). But first, why is creating jobs an urgent requirement? India’s growth story will have little meaning if it fails to create mass jobs, that too in the formal sector. India had 616 million employed people aged 15 years and above, but agriculture accounted for 43% of the figure as against merely 12.1% for manufacturing (Periodic Labour Force Survey, 2025). Even a shift of 1 percentage point employment from agriculture to manufacturing would involve moving a large number of workers. The National Democratic Alliance government had promised to create 20 million jobs every year, but what is has delivered is nowhere near that number. The recent student agitations over paper leaks had an undercurrent of a dearth of respectable jobs in the formal sector. Unemployment among those aged 15-29 years was 9.9%, rising to 13.6% in urban India, while 25% were not in education, employment, or training (PLFS, 2025). Also, female labour force participation was 40%, compared with 79.1% for men. A large share of India’s workforce remains in informal employment, without the stability and social protection of formal jobs. The PLFS usual-status measure includes people who worked for a big part of the year, as well as those who undertook economic activity for at least 30 days. Being counted as “employed” does not necessarily mean having a regular/formal job. For workers to build economic security and resilience, the shift must therefore be towards regular, formal employment with social-security benefits like Employee Provident Fund and Employee State Insurance. This is where the apparel sector matters. It is labour-intensive, employs women in large numbers, and can train workers in short periods — ~60 days for specific production roles. India has set an ambitious target of $100 billion T&A exports by 2030 (from $36 billion today). Of the $100 billion, $40 billion is for apparel exports specifically (currently $15.7 billion). Our interactions with exporters suggest these targets are not grounded in reality. The targets are more likely to be achieved by 2035 than 2030. A positive is that India has recently closed its tariff gaps with competitors like Bangladesh and Vietnam, in major markets such as the EU and the UK. But market access alone does not ensure exports. Take, for example, the 2011 India-Japan trade agreement. India’s apparel exports to Japan fell from $229 million in 2013 to $203 million in 2024. We need the scale and capacity to tap the potential of free trade agreements. The solution is not more factories, but creating a competitive ecosystem around them. Tiruppur, an organically grown knitwear cluster, is perhaps the most compelling example. Its knitwear exports rose from $3.3 billion in 2020-21 to $5.3 billion in 2024-25. The cluster accounts for about 68% of India’s knitwear exports and supports livelihoods of more than a million workers, around 70% of whom are women. Within roughly 20 km, yarn, knitting, dyeing, printing, stitching, finishing, packaging, and dispatch are woven into one production ecosystem. Nearly 20,000 units operate across stages, from knitting, dyeing, and printing to garmenting and ancillary activities. In this ecosystem effect firms and workers specialise and thousands of jobs are created around a common market. So how did Tiruppur do it? Over decades, entrepreneurs, industry associations, and the government built the institutions and common infrastructure that enabled the ecosystem to grow. The Tiruppur Exporters’ Association, under the leadership of A Sakthivel, and the South India Hosiery Manufacturers’ Association played an important role in building collective capabilities, while infrastructure such as the Netaji Apparel Park supported its expansion. The cluster’s collective strength was evident in tackling the environmental crisis. After the Madras High Court’s 2011 order on units failing to meet zero liquid discharge norms, the cluster invested more than `850 crore in common effluent-treatment infrastructure. Tiruppur also shows what it takes to create the next one million jobs. The cluster depends heavily on migrant workers from Odisha, Jharkhand, Bihar, and elsewhere, making worker housing and retention important challenges. The cluster plans to foray into man-made fibres, technical textiles, and high-value sustainable manufacturing to expand both exports and employment. But Tiruppur alone cannot help achieve the target of $100 billion T&A exports by 2030. India needs many more such clusters. Some policy steps in this direction were taken by the government in 2021 with the announcement of seven PM MITRA parks. But till date, only one such park (Warangal) is operational. Such a snail’s pace of execution does not inspire confidence that India can achieve its target of $100 billion exports by 2030. That would also limit the speed at which jobs can be created. ALSO READElectricity, not oil, should define growth Our humble submission is that the Prime Minister needs to give special attention to this sector if we want to create 20 million meaningful jobs annually. Chip-making, AI, and other advanced technologies are important for India’s future, but they are for the highly skilled workforce. A majority of India’s labour force excludes them. The T&A sector offers higher employment intensity at a relatively low cost. China, Bangladesh, and Vietnam have followed that path. India must learn from them. The real test of the Viksit Bharat vision is whether it can create enough productive jobs. T&A offers a clear opportunity, but it needs the PM’s attention to realise it. Ashok Gulati and Sulakshana Rao are a Distinguished Professor and a Senior Fellow at ICRIER, respectively.
