editorials.title: Who will put on the brakes first?
editorials.passage: Artificial intelligence and what it can do has become the flavour of the season. From making humans redundant and changing the nature of work to allowing people to enjoy luxuries that were once unimaginable, and doing things that seemed impossible only a few years ago, AI is now discussed almost every day. There is rarely a day when a technology guru, researcher, or entrepreneur is not analysing another possibility that AI could unlock. ALSO READElectricity, not oil, should define growth But what Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI AI researcher, said recently should make anyone who has been swept up in that excitement sit up. Coxon is no outsider waxing eloquent about the harms of AI. He has worked on AI pretraining at both companies and recently left Anthropic, reportedly giving up equity that had not yet vested. His warning was stark: the companies building the most advanced AI systems are racing towards self-improving superintelligence without having solved how to keep such systems reliably under human control. He has said people working on the technology themselves believe there is a possibility of AI causing catastrophic, even existential, harm within this decade. For an industry that has spent years selling the promise of increasingly capable machines, such a warning is bound to disturb some of the optimism around AI. Now, according to reports, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said the company is open to slowing the development of its AI systems amid growing concerns over the safety of increasingly capable models. And the risks are no longer entirely hypothetical. According to one report, Anthropic said it had disrupted attempts to use its Claude models to support biological weapons research, develop software for missiles and armed drones, and carry out a suspected Russia-linked cyber espionage campaign against the Ukrainian government and military targets. It also said Chinese AI companies had attempted to extract capabilities from its models. So, the companies building frontier AI are beginning to acknowledge that the technology may be moving faster than the safeguards around it. But recognising the problem does not solve it. The bigger question is who slows down first. If OpenAI decides that its next model needs another six months of safety testing while Anthropic or Google continues at full speed, OpenAI could lose its technological lead. If US companies slow down while companies elsewhere continue developing more capable systems, economic competitiveness and national security enter the picture. This is the central problem facing frontier AI. Every company may prefer a world in which the industry develops powerful systems more cautiously. But no company wants to be the only one to do so. There is a familiar historical parallel. During the Cold War, the US and Soviet Union both understood the risks of an unrestricted nuclear arms race. Neither, however, could afford to assume that restraint would be reciprocated. The eventual response was not simply to tell one side to stop, but to create mechanisms through which both sides could place limits on the race. AI is obviously not a nuclear weapon. But the competitive logic has a parallel — everyone may benefit if the race is slowed, while each participant has an incentive to keep running. That is why voluntary restraint has limits. It also explains the growing calls for government intervention. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has already spoken about mandatory testing of advanced AI systems, independent evaluation, and government powers to intervene when systems pose unacceptable risks. There is a strong case for this approach. If the same rules apply to every frontier developer, safety ceases to be a competitive disadvantage. OpenAI does not have to worry that delaying a risky system will hand an advantage to Anthropic, and vice versa. But regulation creates another problem. Governments are being asked to regulate a technology evolving at a pace traditional policymaking is not designed for. For instance, aircraft can be tested against known engineering standards. Medicines go through established clinical and safety procedures. AI is different. A model can acquire new capabilities as it is scaled. A regulator may be trying to certify something whose behaviour is still changing. That does not mean governments should wait until they understand everything about AI. Logically, regulation should focus less on prescribing the technology and more on defining acceptable levels of risk. Automobile provides a useful parallel. Governments did not stop developing more powerful cars because they could be dangerous. They introduced driving licences, speed limits, safety standards, and traffic rules. A similar approach could work for AI. Less capable systems could face lighter requirements, while increasingly autonomous systems face progressively tougher testing and disclosure obligations. However, the difficult part will be deciding where those thresholds lie. Governments will need technical expertise independent of the companies they regulate, access to sufficient information from frontier labs, credible third-party testing, and the ability to revise rules as capabilities change. ALSO READSecuring our skies on our terms There is also a danger that excessively expensive or complicated compliance could strengthen the biggest AI companies by making it harder for smaller competitors to enter the market. So, regulation should set safety conditions, not dictate the pace of innovation. That would perhaps address the industry’s biggest incentive problem and ensure that the company that applies the brakes first is not simply the one that gets left behind. But again, it is difficult to say whether this would work either.

editorials.title: Big-ticket bilaterals
editorials.passage: The highlight of a successful BRICS summit under India’s chairship was no doubt the bilateral meetings of Prime Minister Narendra Modi with the Presidents of Russia and China, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping respectively. These meetings among the founding members of BRICS were highly consequential as they entailed bilateral problem-solving. They took place amid the raging West Asia conflict and unilateral tariff disruption of US President Donald Trump. India has a special and privileged strategic partnership with Russia and is one of the biggest buyers of its oil. Modi and Putin agreed to further strengthen this partnership which has shown “resilience in the backdrop of geopolitical uncertainties”. India’s relations with China are showing signs of a Himalayan thaw. At their meeting, both leaders agreed that the two countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties and differences should not become disputes. Modi and the Russian leader talked about closer trade ties, including the implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030, besides cooperation in energy, infrastructure, technology, defence, and culture. But the major bilateral problem for India is the need for more balance in its trade that is skewed by its dependence on Russian oil, resulting in a high deficit. Both sides resolved to push bilateral trade to $100 billion from current levels of $60 billion by 2030. This is challenging as India would have to massively step up its exports of pharmaceutical, agricultural, and engineering products. Moscow has accumulated a substantial amount of rupees that it has not been able to deploy. The bilateral meeting also discussed cooperation in fertilisers and civil nuclear cooperation. Russian officials indicated possible upgrades of the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile system and supply and production of Su-57 aircraft. The Modi-Xi bilateral was the buzz of the BRICS summit as it involved two of the most important nations of the grouping, whose relations have been in deep freeze due to a border standoff since April 2020. Modi emphasised that peace and tranquillity on the border was essential for improved bilateral relations. As there is now a semblance of peace — despite reports of tension in Arunachal Pradesh — institutional exchanges have gradually resumed and the cooperation list has continued to lengthen. Here again, a major bilateral problem highlighted by Modi was the critical need to address the “structural trade imbalance” due to India’s massive bilateral deficit because of its dependence on imports of industrial inputs, machinery, and electric components, among others, from China. India’s exports face market access barriers. However, the Modi-Xi meeting readouts do not mention India’s policy on foreign direct investment from China which has seen some relaxation of late. While China wants more relaxation of investment restrictions, India may link any further easing to progress on resolving the border dispute. India, for its part, is also concerned about the dragon’s export controls on rare earths and magnets needed for electric and hybrid vehicles. There are also restrictions on the export of ingots, wafer technology, battery cells, and cell technology. For such reasons, India’s relations with China remain fraught. Nevertheless, it is a major positive that meetings are taking place at the highest political levels of both nations. Bilaterals of India with Russia and China may have dominated the conversation at the summit, but they strengthen BRICS as a grouping. India and China getting together is also transformational for the world economy.

editorials.title: The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war
editorials.passage:
“I will not send you to fight and die in stupid foreign wars that never end,” Donald Trump promised a crowd in Pennsylvania in 2024. While the disastrous conflict in Iran, which has escalated in recent days, may make it seem like the president has reneged on that promise, that’s inaccurate. It would be wrong to say that the president has dragged the US into yet another disastrous forever war in the Middle East because, as government officials keep insisting, what’s happening in Iran isn’t actually a war.

“I wouldn’t call it a war,” JD Vance told reporters early this month , for example, after being asked whether the fighting in Iran might be over by the November midterms. “Right now, there is no active shooting.”

Maybe not, but there has been quite a bit of active bombing. Earlier this month, a US missile strike hit a wedding at a private home in southern Iran, killing at least four people, including a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old. That’s fairly restrained compared to the massacre in March when a US precision-guided missile hit an elementary school in Iran, killing 150 people, including 120 children , but it’s still something I would personally file under “possible war crimes”.

But not only does the Trump administration keep insisting this isn’t a real war, they’re also adamant there aren’t any real crimes being committed: the vice-president would like to stress that you shouldn’t believe your eyes or ears when it comes to the civilian deaths being reported. Despite a weapons expert and a visual analysis by the New York Times concluding that the bomb that hit the wedding party in a residential area of the country was American, Vance has a hunch the whole thing might have been made up by some untrustworthy brown people.

“The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,” Vance said at that same press briefing, in relation to the wedding massacre. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”

The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it? A little skirmish? An interminable series of special military operations? A very bloody screw-up? Trump himself has called it a war on several occasions. Last Wednesday, for example , he said: “The war is going to end immediately after the election.” However, rather confusing matters, he also recently suggested he agreed with Vance that it wasn’t a full-fledged war. “I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump said last month. Those are some very expensive potatoes: the not-a-war already has a price tag of tens of billions . Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, has roughly estimated that it has cost the typical US household $1,200. And then of course there’s the human cost: the thousands of lives that have been lost.

What we call this “military conflict” isn’t just semantics, it matters greatly. Not least because the constitution is very clear that a president can’t unilaterally start an official war on a whim; only Congress has the power to declare a war. Trump isn’t the first president to launch major military action without going to Congress for a declaration: Harry Truman classified the Korean conflict as a “police action” to bypass Congress and presidents since have engaged in similar semantic sleights-of-hand. But, as the historian and foreign relations expert Fredrik Logevall noted in an interview with the Harvard Kennedy School: “What’s extraordinary about President Trump in the current context is that he has not really bothered to even consult with Congress, never mind seek the approval of Congress.” In other words, he’s acting like a dictator.

Trump, to be fair, has been clear that he’s exploiting the Truman Playbook. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say if you use the word ‘war,’ that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” Trump said at a fundraising dinner in March. “They don’t like the word ‘war’ because you’re supposed to get approval. So, I’ll use the word ‘military operation’, which is really what it is. It’s a military decimation.”

Avoiding a formal declaration of war might also help the US government bypass certain “wartime” obligations to its service members and their families. Libby Klinner, the widow of an airman killed in combat operations against Iran in March, recently posted on Instagram that she wasn’t receiving certain benefits because the US wasn’t technically at war.

“The Air Force recently told me that because we haven’t officially declared war, my kids and I aren’t eligible for some benefits,” Klinner wrote . “So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we’re left with are being dictated by semantics and public perceptions.”

After this post went viral, it seems the government has stepped in smooth things over. Vance recently said the administration would ensure Klinner receives “what she is entitled to.” He added: “We will certainly work that on the back end.”

The government might be able to fix Klinner’s benefits, but they’re going to have a hard time remedying the economic and political damage this not-a-war is inflicting. Trump’s popularity is plummeting, and a majority of Americans are fed up with this “small potatoes” conflict that has been going on for six months and making everyday life more dangerous and expensive. According to an estimate from Brown University last week, the conflict has cost Americans $100bn in extra energy costs. That bill is going up by $1m every two minutes. This week oil prices also climbed over $100 a barrel for the first time since July.

Meanwhile, with hostilities escalating and no off-ramp in sight, it looks like Trump is out of options. All he has left is empty promises. The president has insisted that energy prices will tumble “right after the election” and, in a sign he is completely desperate, promised every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. The Trump administration can call the war whatever they like, but future generations will define it as a disastrous act of hubris.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: The US right still paints Muslims as the ‘enemy’. But they are fighting for a brighter future for Americans
editorials.passage:
T wenty-five years after 9/11, two pieces of journalism, describing two different phenomena in contemporary New York, tell us a great deal about a city, and indeed a world, caught between two eras. In one, New York Magazine dives into “ Habibi City ”, a New York where a “cultural shift is underway, led by a generation of New Yorkers coming into its own”. This new generation is labelled as originating in “SWANA” – south-west Asia and north Africa, a region that “includes countries from Palestine to Iran to Sudan”. In the other, Vanity Fair describes calls for Zohran Mamdani to not attend the 9/11 memorial ceremony as partly founded in “inchoate, emotional” impulses, that see “the city’s first Muslim mayor as a stand-in for the 19 Muslims who hijacked four planes and turned them into deadly weapons, part of the ‘them’ who attacked ‘us’.”

Together they capture what has changed over a generation, and what remains stubbornly the same. Members of a diaspora of Muslim background are indeed breaking through and accumulating, as New York Magazine says, “clout”. They are no longer simply a fixture of bodegas and halal carts, but of Saturday Night Live, upmarket dining, entertainment and politics too. Mamdani is both the expression of that cohort and the catalyst of its recognition as an emerging force. They care deeply for their local communities but also for those in Gaza and beyond.

I use the descriptor “of Muslim background” rather than “Muslim” because this diasporic identity is a diverse one that is rooted in a religion but expands to encompass everyone from the practising to those for whom Islam is a cultural totem.The capaciousness of this heritage is demonstrable in its integration – without compromise – into mainstream American society. Mamdani and the Democratic Senate nominee for Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, recuse themselves from the rote fealty to American glory and dare to point out both US support for Israel and the calamitous outcomes of the “war on terror” in the Middle East.

This is the result of this new generation of Americans coming from an immigrant background that has cultivated a less parochial and supremacist view of the US. There is something historically inevitable in this. Immigration from countries and backgrounds against which the US has waged military and ideological war eventually yields not a cowed assimilation, but a sort of political cosmopolitanism – kryptonite for American exceptionalism.

Growing up in the shadow of Islamophobia is another formative experience that ironically forced many to identify in terms of religious background rather than race or national origin. “In a way,” said American comedian Ramy Youssef, in a now legendary standup comedy segment , “9/11 made me more Muslim. Cos I was told it was my fault.” This is a profoundly recognisable story for many, including myself, for whom a casual religious identity became a sharp political one during the “war on terror” years.

At the same time as this new generation found their political and social power, the Islamophobia that began in 2001 has only further burrowed into the fabric of American society. Pew research found that, a quarter of a century after 9/11, “public attitudes toward Islam have become more ‘negative’ and more ‘partisan’” than they were in the wake of the attack. In March 2002, 25% of US adults believed that Islam “is more likely than other religions to encourage violence”. Today that figure has doubled to 51%. That is why Mamdani can be seen as a representative of hijackers (despite the fact that he was nine years old on 9/11) and El-Sayed can be called a “terrorist” by Senator Tommy Tuberville. Congresswoman Nancy Mace said that “every single Muslim holding public office in America” is a “threat to both national security and our republic”. “Jihadists”, said Donald Trump, were “being elected all over the place”.

Rozina Ali, the author of Seasons of Fury , a study of the history of Islamophobia in the US, tells me that contemporary Islamophobia cannot be separated from a wider failure of American politics at home and abroad. The “war on terror” turned into a foreign quagmire. At home, a financial crisis saw millions of people lose their homes and savings. One of the reasons Islamophobia has been used by the right is that “a lot of these things can be explained by so called invasions from foreigners or a foreign culture like Islam”. The right, she said, simply “doesn’t have an effective vision for this country that can actually solve a lot of the ills”.

The problem for this approach is not only that Muslims are no longer keeping their heads down, but that they represent a broader progressive politics. Political candidates as well as cultural figures are mobilising large blocks of voters and backers because their worldview has been informed by profound marginalisation. They can root their politics in material concerns about standards of living as well as unpopular foreign policy, in addition to humanising the toll of the political backlash against Muslims and making it a part of the American story. They can unite a broad coalition of people because they too experience being on the losing side against a political establishment.

Despite all the vitriol from the right, anti-Muslim propaganda has not prevented these connections being formed. At the 9/11 commemorative ceremony this past weekend, Mamdani soberly and graciously shook the hand of Rudy Giuliani, the man who was mayor of New York on 9/11, and who had called for Mamdani not to attend. One man was the past, and the other was the future.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism?
editorials.passage:
To imagine the future as being almost entirely bleak has somehow crept into the collective this year.

Last week I was having coffee with an old friend. He was telling me about what his kids wanted to study when they went to university, when he suddenly broke off, stared into the middle distance and said, “I wish I never had children.”

He’d been a father for 20 years and I’d never heard him say that.

He loves his kids beyond measure, but right at that moment, he looked desolate.

It could have been anything AI-related at this point in time. Was it that AI was going to take all the jobs his kids would have done, rendering their lives impoverished and without purpose or meaning? Or was it environmental, with all the water and energy AI consumes that is going to create further stress on the climate and make the planet uninhabitable? Or was it the news that week that AI could “ kill all humans ” within the next 10 years?

It was the latter. We talked listlessly about the killing all humans thing for a bit, then moved on. But the shadow had fallen and I started wondering: is the polycrisis that we are facing so overwhelming that we don’t even have the capacity to talk about it with urgency any more? Instead it’s just there, in the air, ambient, like pollution, each particle containing its own particular doomsday scenario – and the only way to be in this atmosphere, is to be numb to it.

Currently, for so many, all our past and future decisions are being refracted through this strange and dark moment.

If you’re middle-aged – it looks like my friend, wishing (for a moment) you’d never brought kids into the world. Or it might be wondering if it’s worth continuing to work, if you’re not going to be able to enjoy a normal retirement.

If you’re young – it looks like being unable to pick a university degree or vocation because you don’t know what professions or trades will be obsolete in a few years. Or wondering if it’s worth sacrificing and saving for an enormous house deposit, if you won’t have a proper job or future to service a 30-year mortgage.

And if you’re older – it’s being grateful that you won’t be around to see it all unravel.

There are several answers, or ways out of this nihilism we now face – and none of them will be provided by tech.

The first is to wake up. Usually if someone was actually trying to kill you - if they broke into your house and tried to murder you, you would fight back.

Yet we greet the news that AI could cause human extinction with a glazed indifference.

It’s worth remembering that no one actually asked for AI, and yet here it suddenly is trying to kill us. And even if that’s averted, it’s embedding itself in our workplaces and in our emotional lives (GPT may be the largest provider of mental health services in the US), robbing us of the capacity for critical thinking, and threatening economic and social stability.

Why are we so numb in the face of what is – currently – a preventable threat?

This numbness could be the result of almost 20 years of smartphones and social media where, addicted to entertainment, our attention spans have been shortened, and through our individualised algorithms, our capacity for organisation and collective action have been diminished.

Or it could be the huge political power tech companies have that means all of us - including governments feel powerless, or have been captured by big tech.

It could be that the tide of this thing – this progress, the Last Invention – feels inevitable, and like the Luddites storming the factories, any resistance is ultimately useless.

The next solution, after we wake up, is to return to first principles. What are the ingredients for human flourishing? Once we can articulate that, it’s like a rope that can guide us back to where we should be.

Human flourishing is not having a machine to do your critical thinking for you – rather, it’s to engage in the pleasure and the pain of working things out for yourself.

Flourishing is human-to-human relationships where we care for and nurture each other. It’s not talking to a LLM for 18 hours a day about our personal problems.

Flourishing is having a direct relationship with the natural world – not the world through a screen, or the natural world itself destroyed and degraded to create more capacity for screen-based existence.

These are all things worth fighting for. There is a place for technology in our world, it’s just that when we start hearing that it could destroy our world, we should wake up, shake off that numb feeling and start fighting back.

Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the Sage

editorials.title: One Nation’s immigration policy deserves serious discussion – but not for the reason you might think
editorials.passage:
The surprising thing about One Nation’s new immigration policy is not that it contains extreme ideas. It is that parts of it deserve serious discussion.

The best part is its pledge to regulate the size and composition of the temporary migrant population.

This is the right number to target because it links directly to problems people care about, including poor planning, obstacles to integration and migrant worker exploitation.

It is also feasible to contain. Its size is determined by two flows a government can control: the net intake of people on temporary visas, and the number who convert to permanent status.

If these flows are kept equal, the temporary population stabilises. This is not a theory or forecast. It is a mathematical fact.

By contrast, recent political debate has focused on net overseas migration (Nom): the difference between migrant arrivals and departures.

Nom provides a rough measure of all migration. So to claim Nom is the problem supports the false conclusion that all migration is problematic.

It is not. Some parts cannot and should not be regulated, such as movements of Australian citizens. Others, such as permanent migration, are already well regulated. Temporary migration, by contrast, was deregulated 25 years ago and now needs reviewing.

Regulating temporary migration means controlling how many temporary migrants arrive, how long they stay, how many leave and how many become permanent residents. This is all possible under existing legislation. What is changing is the political consensus about whether it is desirable.

Following Canada’s lead in regulating the temporary migrant population could help Australia avoid the problems of previous “guest worker” programs. One Nation deserves credit for putting this on the table.

Beyond this, however, its policy jumps from real problems to blunt, kneejerk cuts that would do more harm than good.

First, it proposes reducing the temporary migrant population by 750,000 over three years by pushing net overseas migration into negative territory.

That is extraordinarily radical. We tried it recently – and it went badly.

Australia last recorded negative net overseas migration during the Covid border closure. Businesses failed, the economy contracted sharply and governments spent massively to cushion the shock. Deliberately recreating that outcome makes little sense.

Second, One Nation’s approach to departures is too punitive. Australia has the right to enforce its immigration laws, and people without a lawful basis to remain have to leave.

But a three-month deadline backed by aggressive enforcement and lifetime re-entry bans raises questions about proportionality and due process. Families, children, long residence and legal processes make cases more complicated than a blanket rule allows.

A migration system must be enforceable, fair and humane. The one-off Covid cohort requires a mix of conversion to permanence for some, extended temporariness for others and, for a few, incentives to depart once visas expire. The objective should be harm minimisation, not an arbitrary net migration target.

Third, there is a racial dimension that cannot be ignored.

One Nation has a long history of framing migration through racial and cultural division. That does not make every question it raises illegitimate. It is reasonable to argue migration is too high or temporary migration needs tighter regulation.

But blaming particular ethnic or religious communities for housing shortages, pressure on services, falling living standards, crime or security threats is analytically weak and socially corrosive. There is a crucial distinction between debating migration policy and blaming migrants.

A better policy would stabilise the system after Covid and tackle the long-term imbalance between permanent and temporary migration. Both require governing the temporary population deliberately.

We should collectively decide how large it should be, what purposes it serves, and where pathways should end. People should either leave when their temporary purpose has ended or, where Australia’s need and their connection have become permanent, have a realistic pathway to permanence.

Australia once led the world in migration research and policymaking, but that capability has eroded . It needs an independent national migration research institute to produce authoritative data, model competing proposals and test political claims against evidence.

Migration is too important to be governed by slogans, arbitrary numbers or scapegoats. If Australia wants a system that commands public confidence, it needs a better-informed debate about what migration is for and how it should be governed.

Alan Gamlen is a professor at the School of Regulation and Global Governance at the Australian National University and director of the ANU Migration Hub

editorials.title: Phone coverage across the London tube? That’s sent me hurtling down a tunnel of despair
editorials.passage:
R ejoice! For by the end of 2026, 4G and 5G mobile coverage is expected across the whole London underground network . After months of delays and setbacks, 121 subterranean tube stations will be dragged kicking and screaming into the 21st century, joining Paris and Berlin in perma-connectivity bliss. But should we really be so happy about the rollout?

Going deep underground was once a way of escaping the incessant communications of this exhausting modern life. Emails to respond to? WhatsApp messages piling up? The tube used to be one of the last remaining bastions of resistance against the constant expectation to do. To optimise. A simpler place where you could justifiably and believably ignore messages and reply later with a “sorry, I was on the tube”.

I see the economic arguments for being better connected. Of course it’s good for business for us to be “on” all the time. And yes, I’ll admit, it is stressful when you get stuck in a tunnel and can’t let your boss know you’re running late. The rollout will also host the new Emergency Services Network (ESN), which will allow first responders to access vital information in an emergency – you can’t argue with that. And, credit where credit is due, the project inarguably represents a remarkable feat of engineering , involving 700 staff and the rollout of hundreds of miles of fibre cabling in the tube’s ancient tunnels.

But on an individual level, what good comes from permanent online connectedness? Studies have shown it’s really bad for our health. Perhaps you’ll be able to leave the office earlier if you’ve got ahead with your work during your morning commute. But it horrifies me that if clients want an instant response, or a bad boss is contacting you out of hours, there’ll soon be nowhere to plausibly hide. I know, I know, lots of people are already living in this brave new world. The tube has 60% connectivity as it is, and lots of commuters who use train networks outside London are used to tethering to a phone or connecting to the train wifi to get ahead on work during their journey. But wasn’t our inability to do the same once a huge point in Londoners’ favour? Yes, the tube is a sweaty sardine can but at least you could lose yourself in a (pre-downloaded) podcast or a book for half an hour, instead of fielding Slack messages from your colleagues.

I can’t understand why we aren’t all more perturbed by this frightening normalisation of being always on. We should be railing against it with all our might. Why must every minute of our time be accounted for? Boredom and daydreaming are good for our brains – we should all be doing more of that.

I’m aware that I sound like a luddite. And I know lots of people find it exceedingly useful being able to work through their to-do list in those idle minutes between leaving the house and arriving somewhere else. But it’s becoming abundantly clear with every new alarmist study that we need saving from ourselves when it comes to our phone addiction. After a day at work and one too many soul-sucking conversations with colleagues, who has the self-discipline not to doom scroll all the way down the Central line? Not me, that’s for sure.

And people can’t be trusted to use this newfound perma-connectivity politely either. My colleague Dan Hancox has recently been bemoaning the “astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK to surf the slopwave without headphones” – a phenomenon that has become noticeably and obnoxiously worse since the tube got internet. And don’t get me started on the number of people talking on the phone on loudspeaker these days. Must we all be made to listen to everyone’s personal conversations on the tube now too? Is this the future?

Give it up, I hear you say. That ship has already sailed. Maybe. But I don’t have to be pleased about it.

Lucy Pasha-Robinson is a Guardian assistant Opinion editor

editorials.title: ​Bangsamoro’s parliamentary election is a turning point
editorials.passage:
On Monday, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the Philippines will hold its first parliamentary election since it was established in 2018. The vote will officially mark the end of the transition period under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), an interim regional government appointed in 2019.

The election is a significant milestone in the Bangsamoro struggle. It is the outcome of decades of armed conflict and negotiations between the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the government of the Philippines.

The vote will test the Philippine government’s commitment to the peace process and the MILF’s commitment to the democratic process.

BARMM is located on Mindanao, the second-largest island in the Philippine Archipelago, and it covers roughly the territories inhabited by the Moro people, a native Muslim-majority group. For centuries, the Moro enjoyed self-governance in independent states and resisted Spanish colonialism. Following the Philippines’s independence in 1946, they continued their struggle for self-determination.

In 1989, the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) was created by Manila to give some devolved rights to the Moro. However, ARMM largely failed to address local grievances and demands due to its weak structural power. It was given limited autonomy in political and fiscal decision-making, but it did not manage to improve socioeconomic conditions in the region. The MILF continued the armed struggle.

In 2012, President Benigno Aquino III recognised the ARMM as a “failed experiment”. Under his administration, the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro was signed between the government and the MILF, paving the way for a new political entity.

Six years later, under President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, the Organic Law for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was promulgated. This legislation granted the region greater fiscal autonomy, a regional government, a parliament, and a justice system.

Then the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro was concluded to outline the mechanism of transition from ARMM to BARMM and set up the MILF-dominated BTA to lead it. All of this is culminating in the parliamentary election, which will determine the makeup of the region’s first legislative body.

The vote comes at a time of heightened tensions in BARMM and internal divisions within the MILF. Two camps have emerged within the movement – one loyal to MILF Chair Al Haj Murad Ebrahim and another supporting Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua.

Last month, Macacua joined the newly formed Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), which will compete in the elections against the MILF’s political wing, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP). Shortly after, his convoy was attacked, but he survived unscathed.

In early September, Macacua and 40 commanders were dismissed from the MILF’s military wing for alleged insubordination.

These tensions have prompted increased public anxiety about possible post-election unrest. There are other factors that could overshadow the vote.

In past elections, vote-buying was widespread, election-related violence was rampant, and electoral fraud and manipulation were pervasive. If these practices repeat at a large scale, the electoral outcome may not necessarily provide a straightforward measure of the will of Bangsamoro’s people. It may also not be an accurate reflection of whether they are satisfied with the transitional government or not.

The MILF presents itself as a champion of moral governance. If it is to retain this label, it should not give in to widespread vote-buying and electoral manipulation. It should also not let internal rivalries turn violent.

But there are already some alarming signs. Prominent MILF figures have conveyed that if the UBJP, the front’s political wing, sees manipulation and fraud, its members are ready to fight. They have also suggested that since the MILF led the transition, it should remain in power. On social media, some citizens have condemned the MILF camp’s threats, calling such tactics un-Islamic.

Before the vote, Manila has deployed military forces in key areas. This has heightened people’s fears that fighting with the MILF may erupt. The tense situation might lead to a low voter turnout.

Under these circumstances, the future of the Bangsamoro is riddled with uncertainties.

Whatever happens in the election, we must remember that the future of BARMM is a shared responsibility. The Philippine government and the Bangsamoro parties are duty-bound to honour the peace agreement. In addition, the people must exercise their civic rights and responsibilities to help sustain the peace achieved after a long and painful armed conflict and to move toward a prosperous Bangsamoro land.

editorials.title: PM Modi’s BRICS masterclass shows how real diplomacy is done
editorials.passage:

South Africa was added subsequently in 2010. These were the countries expected to be the world’s leading nations by 2050. The BRICS nations sought to maintain their own identity and remain neutral, rather than aligning with a particular power bloc. T he acronym BRIC , was first coined by Goldman Sachs economist John O’Neil in 2001; it referred to the international organisation comprising Brazil, Russia, India and China. South Africa was added subsequently in 2010. These were the countries expected to be the world’s leading nations by 2050.

The BRICS nations sought to maintain their own identity and remain neutral, rather than aligning with a particular power bloc. With regional alliances taking place and grouping and ungrouping of different countries with different associations and different interests, a layperson might’ve assumed that the BRICS was not gaining much traction.

The BRICS nations sought to maintain their own identity and remain neutral, rather than aligning with a particular power bloc.

With regional alliances taking place and grouping and ungrouping of different countries with different associations and different interests, a layperson might’ve assumed that the BRICS was not gaining much traction.

And yet, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi managed to pull off a coup of sorts this weekend in New Delhi, with the 18th Summit , held on 12 and 13 September. Chinese President Xi Jinping , Russian President Vladimir Putin, and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa , as well as Brazi l’s Foreign Minister, Mauro Vieira flew into the Indian capital. Apart from the core members , Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, and Abu Dhabi’s Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (representing the UAE) attended the Summit under the personal invitation of PM Modi. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev also participated . After the weekend, it is clear that BRICS is rapidly emerging as an extremely influential group. It aligns 11 major emerging world economies, which together represent nearly 49.5 per cent of the world’s population; approximately 40 per cent of global GDP and nearly 30 per cent of global trade. But w hat makes BRICS relevant today? I have been associated with BRICS and have had the opportunity to work with its different cultural and economic committee s. In the run-up to the Summit, I have had the opportunity to speak across multiple forums: Economic, innovation, artificial intelligence, investment, sustainability and clean energy. During my time interacting with the press and world leaders, I realised that the organisation is as relevant today as it was a quarter of a century ago. “BRICS has emerged as a key platform for coordinating economic policy among major emerging economies. It serves as the principal forum where these nations shape a common position on global governance,” read a PIB report . The organisation has become a “channel for advancing the interests of the Global South”, by using dialogue to promulgate the agenda of finance, development, tech, trade and interpersonal exchange. It seeks to promote the aspirations of developing economies ; to share experiences and face the common challenges together. As the world stares in the face of trade and supply disruptions chains due to regional conflicts, global economic growth suffers. With the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war see ing no end in sight, world trade is in jeopardy due to blockages in various trade routes, and escalating gas prices are affecting all economies, especially those of aspirational countries. Therefore, a bloc which is neutral and chooses not to participate or take sides in a war that belongs to no one is more relevant than ever in the current geopolitical climate . As I said in an ANI interview on the sidelines of the Summit yesterday, with all the disruptions around, diplomacy is something which has been given a chance to survive. Especially now when people have stopped talking to each other, BRICS offers a platform where people can express themselves in a truly democratic way. Whether you agree or disagree is a separate subject and each one has their own perception. Negotiating further pathways for everybody’s well-being is done by listening to others and then finding solutions to the problems. PM Modi made a statement about building for resilience, innovation, climate and sustainability. The message is that while we have to make investments, we have to find alternative mechanisms for financial inclusion and working. Also Read: BRICS is India’s moment. Its neighbours are watching—and worrying about missing out A saner voice Everybody needs a saner voice in the room, where disruption is replaced by diplomacy. For any civilised society to work and progress for the humanitarian cause, it will have to learn to talk and sort out the differences. There will always be differences when ideologies are different, but to navigate diplomacy is the path of reason. How to navigate through those differences is the question, and that is where the influence of BRICS can be seen. Under India’s Presidency, Modi h as set the ball rolling by redefining the purpose of BRICS: Building for resilience, building for climate change, building for world peace, building for innovation, climate and sustainability. BRICS is a methodology offering traction in 3Ts: Technology, trust and trade. In the uncertainty surrounding investments, tariffs, trade issues, disease and epidemics, how you work with each other becomes all the more crucial. The very cause of humanity, international relations and interpersonal dynamics is based on trust, which is a fiduciary relationship. Trust and technology go hand-in-hand and in an increasingly AI-dependent world, technology that can be trusted is the need of the hour. Three cheers for 18th BRICS Summit As leaders depart and the city goes back to normal, the conclusion of the 18th S ummit marks an important moment for the global south and for India’s diplomatic leadership. India’s ability to bring together world leaders such as Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian is no small feat. Further, PM Modi got the BRICS leaders to unequivocally condemn terrorism, with special reference to the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, which took the lives of 25 innocent civilians. The unanimous adoption of the New Delhi Declaration was a substantial 45-page document reflecting consensus among an increasingly diverse BRICS membership. Reaching a unanimous consensus in these volatile geopolitical times of tension, particularly in West Asia, is a significant diplomatic accomplishment. India played an important role in building bridges between differing positions and keeping the group focused on dialogue and cooperation. The summit also strengthened the BRICS agenda on economic cooperation, including greater use of local currencies, more efficient cross-border payment mechanisms and resilience in global supply chains. It emphasised advanced cooperation in AI; an extremely critical achievement after a former Anthropic employee made alarming claims that AI could kill us, likening it to an alien species. The BRICS further suggested aligned thoughts on sharing of critical minerals, health, agriculture, energy, climate action, space, science and technology. They also suggested giving adequate attention to start-ups, MSMEs, skills, and women-led development. India’s successful chairship has demonstrated that BRICS can remain a platform for dialogue even amid profound differences and that the global south is increasingly determined to shape new rules for a new emerging global order. Also Read: BRICS is not a bloc of rising powers. China is hauling it alone A bridge for the world The New Delhi D eclaration was adopted unanimously even though there are some big differences between member nations, especially over the Russia-Ukraine war and a broader relationship with the United States. That is a significant diplomatic achievement, no doubt. India has successfully demonstrated that it can simultaneously talk to Washington, Moscow, Beijing, Tehran, the UAE and the Gulf without formally aligning itself with any one camp. India is a “Vishwa Mitra” (global friend) and a voice for the world . Equally significant was an emphasis on a more representative and multipolar global order, with suggestions of reform of global institutions and a louder, stronger voice for developing countries. The summit’s criticism of unilateral sanctions, protectionism and the existing global financial architecture is significant. The declaration has also pushed for greater representation of developing countries in world leadership institutions such as the UN and global financial institutions. BRICS declaration brought forward a message that institutions working to resolve challenges have to make space for convergence of ideas and rise above individual interests. My special compliments to Iran and the UAE, which came forward in support of the declaration. The Summit produced a common position that called for restraint and de-escalation, while the gathering also created space for direct engagement of different countries. Rather than a military alliance, the focus was on creating a diplomatic space . PM Modi stated at the conclusion of the BRICS Summit 2026 that the grouping has evolved into an “ecosystem of solutions” and emphasised that as BRICS enters its third decade, “the world now expects concrete results from the group, and not just ideas and commitments”. I was invited to kick off a football match organised by the BRICS International Football Alliance (BIFA) and also inaugurate its Delhi chapter. I was reminded that football has a simple rule : Y ou may compete fiercely on the field, but you gotta play by the same rules. BRICS is much like that : d ifferent countries, different interests, different strengths; sometimes very different strategies. But the real game is about finding common ground, creating opportunities and keeping the ball rolling. Because in football, as in geopolitics, no one wins by refusing to pass. Meenakshi Lekhi is a BJP leader and lawyer. Her X handle is @M_Lekhi. Views are personal. (Edited by Insha Jalil Waziri)

editorials.title: The India-China reset will be tested in the Northeast
editorials.passage:
A mid significant geopolitical fragmentation, New Delhi has brought together countries with widely divergent interests to secure the ambitious New Delhi Declaration. The BRICS Summit was everything that India envisioned it to be. It was well coordinated, visually smart, carefully articulated, and achieved a consensus that was particularly significant given tensions within BRICS itself, including the conflict in West Asia and differences between Iran and the UAE. Yet, the grouping arrived at a common declaration and reiterated its commitment to dialogue, multilateralism and a more representative international order. This was important to India as New Delhi has consistently resisted attempts to define BRICS simply as an anti-Western coalition. It prefers to position the grouping as a platform through which emerging economies can gain greater influence over global rule-making while developing practical mechanisms for cooperation.

Yet, the grouping arrived at a common declaration and reiterated its commitment to dialogue, multilateralism and a more representative international order.

This was important to India as New Delhi has consistently resisted attempts to define BRICS simply as an anti-Western coalition. It prefers to position the grouping as a platform through which emerging economies can gain greater influence over global rule-making while developing practical mechanisms for cooperation.

And to that end, Paragraph 5 of the New Delhi Declaration commends India’s 2026 Chairship for its “practical, actionable, inclusive, development-oriented and people-centered approach” built around resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. The Modi-Xi meeting and the India-China reset However, apart from carefully crafting the New Delhi Declaration and navigating the larger BRICS deliberations, the most watched meeting was clearly between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The meeting provided further evidence that the cautious reset of India-China relations is gathering momentum. President Xi’s presence in New Delhi, his first visit to India in seven years, was itself significant. The two leaders discussed greater economic engagement, connectivity and people-to-people exchanges. But PM Modi made clear that any reset remains conditional and that peace and tranquillity along the border are fundamental to rebuilding the wider bilateral relationship. This statement naturally brings one’s attention to India’s northeast. Because if India and China are genuinely entering a period of stabilisation, then the ultimate test will be India’s northeast. Since the Galwan clash of 2020, attention has understandably been concentrated on eastern Ladakh. But the eastern end of the India-China frontier presents a different and, in some ways, a more complicated strategic challenge. China continues to claim almost the entirety of Arunachal Pradesh and calls it Zangnan, periodically issuing Chinese names for locations there. India categorically rejects the claim, calling the provocation ‘preposterous’. More importantly, the northeast is where territorial security intersects with Tibet, transboundary rivers, climate change, border infrastructure and India’s connectivity towards Myanmar and Southeast Asia. The northeast as the test of the reset Even before BRICS, developments pointed towards a step-by-step reset. It was during the 25th Round of the Special Representatives Talks on the India-China Boundary Question in Beijing on August 25 that the two sides reached an eight-point consensus. It included stronger LAC management mechanisms, additional senior military meeting points and military hotlines in the Eastern and Middle Sectors, expanded border exchanges and renewed discussions on transboundary rivers and hydrological data sharing. This exchange between India’s NSA Ajit Doval and China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi was followed by the first-ever senior-most military commander-level flag meetings, against the backdrop of recent tensions around Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh. Taken together with the Modi-Xi meeting, these developments make a compelling case for placing the northeast closer to the centre of India’s China policy. The initial results of these engagements have been positive, with China scaling back troops on the LAC. But a genuine reset still needs to demonstrate that stability can be maintained across the entire frontier. Also Read: Xi-Modi BRICS meeting signals thaw in ties. The Chinese say it is at a fragile stage The Brahmaputra is also a security issue But the northeast has other important challenges beyond stability on the LAC. The Brahmaputra enters India through Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang after flowing through Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo. China’s massive Motuo hydropower ambitions on the river have understandably generated anxiety in India. Though the concern should not be limited to claims that China can simply “switch off” the Brahmaputra, the more immediate problem is the strategic asymmetry emerging when a downstream country depends partly on activities and environmental events occurring upstream. Hydrological data, sediment flows, dam safety, and warnings of exceptional water releases, landslides, or glacial events therefore have serious strategic implications. Climate change adds to the urgency of addressing these issues. Recent extreme weather events across the Himalayas, such as the devastation in Nepal, demonstrated how rapidly glacial instability and landslides can become transboundary problems. For Arunachal Pradesh and Assam, reliable upstream information is no longer a mere environmental issue but a national security requirement. Interestingly, the BRICS New Delhi Declaration provides a framework for precisely this kind of cooperation. Paragraph 113 acknowledges water availability as a critical environmental challenge and calls for the integrated protection and systematic management of mountains and water resources, among other ecosystems. The relevance for India’s northeast is evident, with the eastern Himalayas and the Yarlung Tsangpo-Brahmaputra system bringing precisely these two issues of mountains and water together. The Declaration further states in paragraph 83 the importance of investment in sustainable resilience, prevention and anticipatory action and specifically emphasises stronger early warning systems and risk-informed planning. For a region exposed to glacial instability, landslides, extreme rainfall and transboundary flooding, these principles are directly relevant. India and China have therefore jointly endorsed the broader proposition that climate resilience requires better information, early warning and cooperation. India should use the present thaw to translate those principles into a more predictable bilateral framework for the Yarlung Tsangpo-Brahmaputra. A 21st-century border management framework can no longer concern itself exclusively with soldiers. It must also address water and environmental risks affecting populations downstream. India must simultaneously strengthen its independent satellite surveillance, remote sensing, river gauges and glacier monitoring. Building a resilient frontier But there is yet another reason why the northeast should be central to the reset. Resilient connectivity has been an important component of India’s wider BRICS agenda. For the northeast, the intersection between connectivity and resilience is significant. Roads, bridges, tunnels and telecommunications near the LAC support civilian mobility and economic integration as well as military logistics. In an increasingly unstable Himalayan climate, resilience must become part of strategy. Border villages should not simply be viewed as India’s last settlements before China. They should become India’s first settlements looking outward. Strong local economies, communications, tourism, transport and public services strengthen the frontier as strategically as military infrastructure does. The northeast and India’s Act East strategy The northeast’s importance also extends beyond China. It forms India’s principal land bridge towards Myanmar and Southeast Asia. Projects such as the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and the Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project are therefore more than development projects. They are instruments for integrating the northeast with India’s Act East strategy. China approaches this geography from another direction, with its economic corridors through Myanmar providing southwestern China access towards the Indian Ocean. The northeast consequently sits at the intersection of India’s continental and maritime strategies. China and Tibet to its north, Myanmar to its east and, beyond these, the Bay of Bengal make the northeast a critical strategic bridge between India’s land and maritime interests. If an India-China reset is to happen, India must use this period of stability for accelerated investments. It must not hesitate to venture into new projects for strategic advancement, such as the reopening and construction of the much-debated Ledo Road. Turning the BRICS vision into a northeast strategy This is where the language of the New Delhi Declaration acquires concrete meaning. The resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability emphasised under India’s Chairship in Paragraph 5 translate, in the northeast, to stronger roads and bridges, hydrological and early warning capabilities, institutionalised transboundary cooperation and economically stronger and thriving border communities. The success of the Delhi BRICS Summit demonstrated that India and China can negotiate common positions despite substantial differences. However, the harder test begins after the summit: applying that ability to cooperate to geographical interests. Finally, the real test of the India-China reset will not be in New Delhi but in the northeast. Rami Niranjan Desai is a Distinguished Fellow at the India Foundation, New Delhi. She tweets @ramindesai. Views are personal. (Edited by Maryam Hassan)

This exchange between India’s NSA Ajit Doval and China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi was followed by the first-ever senior-most military commander-level flag meetings, against the backdrop of recent tensions around Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh. Taken together with the Modi-Xi meeting, these developments make a compelling case for placing the northeast closer to the centre of India’s China policy. The initial results of these engagements have been positive, with China scaling back troops on the LAC. But a genuine reset still needs to demonstrate that stability can be maintained across the entire frontier. Also Read: Xi-Modi BRICS meeting signals thaw in ties. The Chinese say it is at a fragile stage The Brahmaputra is also a security issue But the northeast has other important challenges beyond stability on the LAC. The Brahmaputra enters India through Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang after flowing through Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo. China’s massive Motuo hydropower ambitions on the river have understandably generated anxiety in India. Though the concern should not be limited to claims that China can simply “switch off” the Brahmaputra, the more immediate problem is the strategic asymmetry emerging when a downstream country depends partly on activities and environmental events occurring upstream. Hydrological data, sediment flows, dam safety, and warnings of exceptional water releases, landslides, or glacial events therefore have serious strategic implications. Climate change adds to the urgency of addressing these issues. Recent extreme weather events across the Himalayas, such as the devastation in Nepal, demonstrated how rapidly glacial instability and landslides can become transboundary problems. For Arunachal Pradesh and Assam, reliable upstream information is no longer a mere environmental issue but a national security requirement. Interestingly, the BRICS New Delhi Declaration provides a framework for precisely this kind of cooperation. Paragraph 113 acknowledges water availability as a critical environmental challenge and calls for the integrated protection and systematic management of mountains and water resources, among other ecosystems. The relevance for India’s northeast is evident, with the eastern Himalayas and the Yarlung Tsangpo-Brahmaputra system bringing precisely these two issues of mountains and water together. The Declaration further states in paragraph 83 the importance of investment in sustainable resilience, prevention and anticipatory action and specifically emphasises stronger early warning systems and risk-informed planning. For a region exposed to glacial instability, landslides, extreme rainfall and transboundary flooding, these principles are directly relevant. India and China have therefore jointly endorsed the broader proposition that climate resilience requires better information, early warning and cooperation. India should use the present thaw to translate those principles into a more predictable bilateral framework for the Yarlung Tsangpo-Brahmaputra. A 21st-century border management framework can no longer concern itself exclusively with soldiers. It must also address water and environmental risks affecting populations downstream. India must simultaneously strengthen its independent satellite surveillance, remote sensing, river gauges and glacier monitoring. Building a resilient frontier But there is yet another reason why the northeast should be central to the reset. Resilient connectivity has been an important component of India’s wider BRICS agenda. For the northeast, the intersection between connectivity and resilience is significant. Roads, bridges, tunnels and telecommunications near the LAC support civilian mobility and economic integration as well as military logistics. In an increasingly unstable Himalayan climate, resilience must become part of strategy. Border villages should not simply be viewed as India’s last settlements before China. They should become India’s first settlements looking outward. Strong local economies, communications, tourism, transport and public services strengthen the frontier as strategically as military infrastructure does. The northeast and India’s Act East strategy The northeast’s importance also extends beyond China. It forms India’s principal land bridge towards Myanmar and Southeast Asia. Projects such as the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and the Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project are therefore more than development projects. They are instruments for integrating the northeast with India’s Act East strategy. China approaches this geography from another direction, with its economic corridors through Myanmar providing southwestern China access towards the Indian Ocean. The northeast consequently sits at the intersection of India’s continental and maritime strategies. China and Tibet to its north, Myanmar to its east and, beyond these, the Bay of Bengal make the northeast a critical strategic bridge between India’s land and maritime interests. If an India-China reset is to happen, India must use this period of stability for accelerated investments. It must not hesitate to venture into new projects for strategic advancement, such as the reopening and construction of the much-debated Ledo Road. Turning the BRICS vision into a northeast strategy This is where the language of the New Delhi Declaration acquires concrete meaning. The resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability emphasised under India’s Chairship in Paragraph 5 translate, in the northeast, to stronger roads and bridges, hydrological and early warning capabilities, institutionalised transboundary cooperation and economically stronger and thriving border communities. The success of the Delhi BRICS Summit demonstrated that India and China can negotiate common positions despite substantial differences. However, the harder test begins after the summit: applying that ability to cooperate to geographical interests. Finally, the real test of the India-China reset will not be in New Delhi but in the northeast. Rami Niranjan Desai is a Distinguished Fellow at the India Foundation, New Delhi. editorials.title: Kalibangan was hiding in plain sight. It deserves more than a footnote to Harappan history
editorials.passage:
M ore than a century ago, when the Harappan cities still lay buried beneath the earth, when the history of the subcontinent was thought to begin only in the 6th century BCE, and when there was no known evidence of an Indian Bronze Age, an Italian Indologist, traveller and explorer traversed the undulating sand dunes and flat alluvial plains of the erstwhile Bikaner state on camelback. Between 1916 and 1919, Luigi Pio Tessitori, who was entrusted by John Marshall, surveyed this rich landscape marked by ancient mounds along the dry channel of the Ghaggar. Wealth flows from geography Kalibangan: Harappan Frontier in the Thar Kalibangan, the name literally translates to black bangles, is an archaeological site located at the confluence of rivers Ghaggar and Chautang, in present-day Hanumangarh district of Rajasthan. After its initial investigation by Tessitori, the site remained buried both literally and symbolically despite its mention in the survey records of Aurel Stein in the 1940s. Since Stein was unable to identify the site’s cultural affinity, the onus of its recognition fell on Amalananda Ghosh and his team, who surveyed the Bikaner state in the 1950s. Ghosh identified the site as a Harappan settlement and recorded its antiquities. The research questions during this survey did not align with the excavation of Kalibangan, which had to wait till 1961, when it was finally subjected to excavation by the Archaeological Survey of India. Stalwarts of Indian archaeology, including BB Lal, BK Thapar, JP Joshi and others, excavated the site between 1961-1969. Spread over an area of 25 hectares, the site comprises three mounds—KLB 1, KLB 2 and KLB 3. The excavation yielded an Early Harappan deposit at the site for the first time in independent India. According to BK Thapar, Kalibangan was the fourth pre-urban or Early Harappan site to be excavated following the excavation at Amri, Kot Diji and Harappa, which were part of newly formed Pakistan. The Early Harappan level, which is dated to the fifth century BCE, yielded a parallelogram fortified settlement measuring 250m x 180m. The fortification wall was made of mud-bricks (30x20x10cm) in the ratio of 3:2:1 and had two structural phases. Within the walled area, houses with two to three rooms and a courtyard, made with mud bricks and a sophisticated drainage system made of baked brick or terracotta pipes, were found. A lane measuring 1.5 metres in width between two houses was excavated during the early and pre-urban levels. Moreover, a hearth resembling a modern-day tandoor with mud-plastered walls was found, along with cylindrical pits lined with lime plaster, possibly for storing water. Agriculture practises indicated by the infamous furrow marks at the sites and archaeobotanical evidence indicated at cultivation of winter (rabi) crops. And for the antiquities, chert blades, terracotta toy-cart wheel, carnelian and agate beads, and a copper celt were found. During the Mature Harappan (urban phase), the settlement was divided into a citadel found at KBL 1, which was found overlaying the Early Harappan horizon, and a lower city found at KBL 2. Excavators noted that the city layout and the settlement pattern changed during this period. The citadel was a fortified parallelogram measuring 240 x 120m. The fortification was 3 to 7 meters in width and was made of mud-bricks in the ratio of 4:2:1. The lower city was about 40cm away from the citadel and was also fortified. The fortification was 3 to 9 meters wide and within the fortification the city had a gridiron plan of streets running north to south and in the east to west direction. The streets were two to five meters wide. Evidence of houses with multiple rooms, sometimes decorated with stylised terracotta tiles, courtyards, and lanes was found. The drainage system was even more sophisticated, with specialised terracotta pipes, some even bearing Harappan letters were found. The water management system also included wells made with trapezoid-shaped bricks. Evidence of wheat and barley was found, along with the domestication of cattle, which was a continuation from the early phase. The material culture was as vibrant as any other major Harappan city, which had to be accommodated in multiple volumes of the excavation report. An array of terracotta human figurines was found from the site, which is significant as it is a rarity in the eastern domain of the civilisation. Some were decorated and some were also anthropomorphic. An interesting terracotta anthropomorphic figure, resembling a Celt, was found. Apart from human figurines, animal figurines, particularly that of a zebu bull, are a favourite of the people of Kalibangan. Interestingly, bulls are integral to the locality even today, as one can find many grazing on the site or resting under a tree. A copper bull statue is especially significant for its iconography and making. Moreover, a terracotta cake, which is one of the Harappan markers, largely underrated, was found. It had an engraved human figure with horned headgear on one side, and a human figure carrying probably an animal on the other side is interesting and rare. This, as per the excavators, suggest to some belief system among the people, evidence of which was found at KBL 3 on the northeastern edge of the site. It was here that multiple hearths labelled by excavators as fire-altars were found. The absence of any domestic activity in this area and the presence of an isolated mud-brick structure appealed to the excavators as evidence of rituals. Why Kalibangan? While a thesis can be written on the plethora of significant and unique evidence found at the site, it is important to highlight its importance, as the buck often stops at Rakhigarhi these days. Unlike Rakhigarhi, this site was excavated for nine field seasons, which yielded evidence that is unique to the region where it is located. Ancient cities, particularly Harappan cities, were strategically located. Similarly, Kalibangan, literally translated as black bangles, is located near the confluence of Ghaggar and Chautang. According to Gregory Possehl, this city may have played a significant role as a way station and monitor of overland communications of the Harappan people. With over a hundred Harappan sites in the lower Ghaggar basin, the area, which is present-day Sri Ganganagar and Hanumangarh districts of Rajasthan, Kalibangan appears to be a big settlement, located in the middle of the lower Ghaggar River basin. It is approximately 277 km west of Rakhigarhi and 300-320 km east of Ganweriwala, another major Harappan site located in Cholistan but within the Ghaggar-Hakra river Basin. As it was at the confluence of the major river channel and its tributaries, interconnected by smaller but significant Harappan sites, it is possible that Kalibangan was not only a way-station as Possehl suggested but a major centre of trade and authority. The array of material from other Harappan sites is an indicator of the interconnected matrix which is a hallmark of Harappan Civilisation. Protected and preserved The site remained underrepresented in the public domain despite being the only Harappan site in this region to have a decent site museum. Government initiatives to re-excavate the site and build an open-air museum have yielded no results, but as we keep pushing these demands, we have to understand if an open-air site museum would be advisable. Just as dramatic as its discovery and how it was pushed into the background, the site should not be ignored. Kalibangan is not just another site, but represents a fortress of resilience and power in the arid region on the fringes of Thar. Kalibangan is not just another site, but represents a fortress of resilience and power in the arid region on the fringes of Thar. editorials.title: India needs more buildings—and a fresh look at land acquisition financing
editorials.passage:
T he collapse of a five-storey boys’ hostel in Delhi’s Satya Niketan killed seven people and injured several others. Two months ago, a fire in a Malviya Nagar building killed 23 people. Two years ago, the Old Rajinder Nagar basement flooding tragedy killed three UPSC aspirants. Every time something like this happens, especially in metropolitan cities, the prescription is familiar: enforce building codes better, conduct structural audits, crack down on illegal construction, and increase penalties. Another school of thought says the answer is more construction: liberalise Floor Space Index (FSI), make land-use rules less restrictive, allow private developers to build faster. Occasionally, there’s the least useful answer of all: let the government take over building construction. But, there is a question sitting underneath all three arguments that gets surprisingly little attention: who is going to finance the buildings? India does not merely need more or safer buildings. It needs a financial system capable of funding the enormous stock of buildings that urbanisation will require. Land is the largest component of this capital requirement. But our regulatory system imposes structural barriers on financing the acquisition of land by private developers.
