Land is the largest component of this capital requirement. But our regulatory system imposes structural barriers on financing the acquisition of land by private developers.

Under the RBI’s banking regulations , banks may finance virtually every other stage of a development project, from construction to the purchase of completed homes. , But, they remain largely barred from financing the acquisition of the land on which those projects are built. This restricts the scale at which India n developers can realistically construct real estate in our cities. The absence of seed capital for real estate development Consider what happens when a developer decides to construct a large residential or commercial project. There is a fairly obvious sequence: acquire the land, obtain approvals, construct the project, lease or sell the completed asset, and eventually generate a stream of cash flows from it. The financial system should be capable of supporting this entire chain. Indian banks can finance construction. They can finance individuals purchasing homes. They can finance factories, roads, and other infrastructure projects built on land. But, they cannot finance private developers acquiring the land on which residential and commercial projects are to be built. This is not a minor regulatory technicality. Land can account for 50-80 per cent of the cost of real-estate development in major Indian cities. Preventing banks from financing that component creates a structural hole in the financing chain. Resultantly, developers turn to private credit, non-bank lenders, and other forms of financing, often at considerably higher cost, pushing up the cost of constructed real estate. Historically, the financing vacuum around land has also provided fertile ground for unaccounted money and opaque transactions. There is a certain irony here. We worry about speculative land markets and the risks of real-estate lending. So we prohibit the banking system from financing a large part of the land-development cycle — and then leave the financing to parts of the financial system that may be more expensive and less transparent. REITs show what financialisation can do India has already demonstrated that real estate can be converted into a financial asset. The success of listed Real Estate Investment Trusts, or REITs, is an important experiment in this direction. REITs allow investors to own units backed by income-generating real estate rather than having to buy and manage buildings themselves. The model has worked particularly well for Grade-A office assets. India’s listed REIT ecosystem has grown to cover hundreds of millions of square feet of commercial and retail property, with substantial distributions to investors. That said, so far, REIT investments have been concentrated disproportionately in commercial office assets. The much larger universe of urban real estate — rental housing, student hostels , healthcare, senior living, and other specialised assets — has barely been financialised. Indeed, acknowledging the institutional funding gap in real estate, SEBI’s latest discussion paper on REIT s published last month proposes allowing REITs to invest minority stakes in under-construction projects undertaken by developers. This is a step in the right direction. REITs can only take us so far Aggregating land parcels and building residential townships that can be rented out at scale is key to the viability of REITs as financial assets. This forces us to return to the ban on banks financing land. Think of the capital stack for real estate development as a chain: Land acquisition → construction → completion → stabilisation → rental income → REIT → long-term institutional capital. India has been gradually building the downstream parts of this chain. REITs are most suited to come in once rentals and cash flows become visible. But there remains a financing gap right at the beginning. This gap is a significant barrier because urban land is often the single largest component of the cost of development. Also read: Satya Niketan was not an accident. Delhi has a student housing problem From prohibition to prudence The prohibition on bank financing of land acquisition has understandable historical roots. It emerged in an era when Indian banking was state-dominated, land markets were opaque and fragmented, property records were weak, and policymakers were concerned that institutional credit would fuel speculation in land. But India’s financial system has changed. Banking is more market-oriented. Real-estate regulation has changed. RERA has created an institutional framework for monitoring projects and ring-fencing customer money. Financial regulation itself has moved substantially toward risk-based supervision. The question, therefore, is no longer whether land finance is risky. The question is whether prohibition is still the best way to manage that risk. Major advanced economies do not generally deal with the risks of land and real-estate lending through an absolute prohibition. Banks in countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Germany, and Japan can finance land acquisition and development, subject to substantial prudential constraints. A better framework would allow banks to finance land acquisition for bona fide development projects, but only where the project has appropriate approvals, a defined implementation schedule, and meaningful promoter equity. Regulators could impose conservative loan-to-value ratios, higher capital requirements, milestone-based disbursement, commencement deadlines, and enhanced provisioning. They could restrict speculative land banking and impose sectoral or borrower-level exposure limits. Modern prudential regulation has developed these tools to deal with risky lending. A financial market — where banks finance appropriately regulated development, REITs provide a route to long-duration institutional capital, and prudential regulation controls rather than prohibits risk — is as important as building more and safer buildings. The lesson from India’s recent building tragedies should certainly be that enforcement matters. But there is a second lesson. India’s cities cannot be made safer, larger or more liveable merely by writing better building rules. Someone has to finance the buildings that comply with them. Regulation determines what can be built. Finance determines what actually gets built. And as India urbanises, Indian financial architecture will have to rise to this challenge. For starters, let’s abandon old tropes and taboos on land financing. Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah is the co-founder and CEO of The Professeer. She tweets @bhargavizaveri. Harsh Vardhan is a management consultant and researcher based in Mumbai. Views are personal. (Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)

India has already demonstrated that real estate can be converted into a financial asset. The success of listed Real Estate Investment Trusts, or REITs, is an important experiment in this direction. REITs allow investors to own units backed by income-generating real estate rather than having to buy and manage buildings themselves. The model has worked particularly well for Grade-A office assets. India’s listed REIT ecosystem has grown to cover hundreds of millions of square feet of commercial and retail property, with substantial distributions to investors.

That said, so far, REIT investments have been concentrated disproportionately in commercial office assets. The much larger universe of urban real estate — rental housing, student hostels , healthcare, senior living, and other specialised assets — has barely been financialised. Indeed, acknowledging the institutional funding gap in real estate, SEBI’s latest discussion paper on REIT s published last month proposes allowing REITs to invest minority stakes in under-construction projects undertaken by developers. This is a step in the right direction. This forces us to return to the ban on banks financing land. editorials.passage:
A nyone who has driven along the western seaboard over the past decade knows the subtle friction of India’s economic geography. Between the industrial powerhouses of Gujarat and the tranquil estuarine towns of the Konkan, an immense logistical transition is taking place. For decades, the national economic narrative belonged to the inland trunk routes — principally National Highway 48, the multi-lane spine that threads the Delhi-Mumbai industrial corridor through Rajasthan and Gujarat down into peninsular India, and east-west arteries like NH-53 that draw heavy freight from the mineral belts of central India to western ports. Along Gujarat’s maritime edge, dedicated industrial corridors like NH-64 and vital feeder arteries like NH-848 link petrochemical zones and deep-draft terminals directly into this continental grid. Further south, spurs like NH-160 around the Mumbai-Nashik threshold siphon manufacturing output from the hinterland toward coastal exit points. Yet the real pressure test of modern Indian transport planning is no longer occurring on the wide, open plains of the interior. It is gathering along the narrower, ecologically delicate coastal ribbon serviced by National Highway 66.

Connecting Navi Mumbai through Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, and down to the southern tip at Kanyakumari, NH-66 was once envisioned as a picturesque coastal highway. Today, it has become an economic conduit of extraordinary density. Along this strip sits what can best be termed the Tier-2 Coastal Carrying Capacity Paradox. The very geography that makes these coastal towns economically magnetic — their ports, river mouths, maritime climate, and scenic topography — strictly limits their spatial expansion. Caught between the Arabian Sea and the steep escarpments of the Western Ghats, these urban centres cannot sprawl in concentric circles like Indore, Hyderabad, or Lucknow. At the same time, they are experiencing a rapid, concurrent surge of tourism, port logistics, light manufacturing, real estate development, and institutional services. When container trailers from maritime hubs, holidaymakers in rented hatchbacks, interstate commercial carriers, and daily office commuters all converge on the same coastal corridors, the friction does not merely cause temporary traffic snarls. It hits a structural wall. The limits of horizontal widening For many years, the response of policy-makers to any transport bottleneck has been rather simple : expand the blacktop. However, for the coastal stretch, traditional horizontal expansion of roads has come to a natural end. The land next to these routes is highly valued, politically charged, and environmentally sensitive. The process of expanding a route horizontally would mean destroying the ancestral homes, breaking into well-established retail business centers, cutting down old tree canopies, and facing extreme land fragmentation. Land acquisition in densely populated areas along the coast proves to be too costly and time-consuming. This is where planners are faced with the harsh realities of life: we have to expand vertically when expanding horizontally becomes unsustainable. Goa offers a telling lens into this dilemma. Over the past five years, the state has absorbed capital expenditure on infrastructure at an unprecedented scale. Signature river crossings like the New Zuari Bridge and the Atal Setu over the Mandovi have bypassed historical bottlenecks, while upgraded highways have knitted together mining clusters, industrial estates in Verna and Kundaim, and coastal tourism belts. Yet the commissioning of Manohar International Airport at Mopa in North Goa immediately shifted the gravitational pull of traffic. The arterial stretch of NH-66 between Panaji, Porvorim, and Mapusa — which feeds this northern gateway — found itself handling a volatile mix of high-speed airport transit, commercial supplies, inter-city passenger traffic, and local residential commutes. The solution currently taking shape along this stretch — the 5.15-km, six-lane elevated corridor through Porvorim — embodies this necessary engineering shift. By lifting through-traffic several metres into the air within the existing highway right-of-way, the project doubles corridor throughput without consuming adjacent private land. The use of precast segmental construction here is not merely an engineering detail; it is a civic imperative. Cast in off-site yards and launched girder-by-girder overhead, precast segments compress multi-year construction timelines and spare living urban neighbourhoods the suffocating, business-killing dust and disruption of protracted ground-level excavation. Elevated viaducts, however, cannot become deaf concrete monoliths that bisect communities. An elevated road succeeds only if the space underneath is deliberately integrated: with grade-level pedestrian crosswalks, local access lanes, intelligent drainage to withstand ferocious monsoon cloudbursts, sound barriers near residential zones, and well-lit public recreational spaces carved out beneath the pier caps. Also read: India’s east coast handles a higher volume. But the west coast has better economic outcome The logistics multiplier and the multi-modal shift The urgency of solving these urban bottlenecks extends far beyond commuter comfort; it goes to the heart of the national economy. An urban bottleneck in public finance is never merely an issue of transit; it is a regressive tax on economic productivity. Fuel used up in first gear by idling freight vehicles waiting to unload cargo at the port, clogged taxis at airport hubs, and service workers trying to navigate bottleneck corridors all cost the economy, whether in the form of higher logistics costs, prolonged inventory holding periods, unreliable delivery schedules, or loss of attractiveness of the destination for high-value services. For Goa, Mangaluru, Surat, and other tier-2 coastal towns, the way forward has got to be a bold multi-modal transit strategy. Airport corridors, rail terminals, ferry jetties, and bus terminals have got to integrate in some kind of schedule-based feeder network. With electric buses and feeder shuttles running frequently enough, the arrival at an airport or rail terminal will no longer imply the need for putting another single-passenger car out on the highway. By combining peripheral park-and-ride centers with public transportation, cities may preserve the unique heritage and environmental attraction of the city itself. India’s coastal economic growth cannot simply be paved over. The sea on one side and the hills on the other remind us that land is a finite gift. How intelligently we engineer the third dimension — and how swiftly we link our roads to a broader transit fabric — will decide whether these coastal cities remain engines of prosperity or choke under the weight of their own promise. Savio Rodrigues is a BJP State Executive Member, political analyst, and national commentator & expert on Goa affairs. Views are personal. (Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)

editorials.title: Russia and India are building a new pole of attraction in global energy
editorials.passage:
T he Russian Arctic continental shelf is one of the world’s most promising territories for hydrocarbon extraction . P reliminary estimates suggest it holds up to 25 per cent of global reserves—a potential energy security guarantee for Europe and beyond for decades to come. Current assessments put the forecast hydrocarbon potential of Russia’s Arctic shelf at roughly 100 billion tonnes of oil equivalent. Since 2022, India has become one of the most important markets for Russian oil, rapidly rising to become the second-largest buyer after China . T oday , it purchas es up to 60 per cent of Russia’s seaborne crude exports. India is also the world’s second-largest exporter of refined petroleum products to Europe, meaning Russia-India cooperation now plays a direct role in the energy security of a wide range of countries. In September 2023, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, attending the Eastern Economic Forum, signalled India’s interest in cooperating with Russia on energy and Arctic matters. Since 2020, India has participated in the Vostok Oil project, developing new oil fields on the Taymyr Peninsula. Crude extracted in northern Krasnoyarsk Krai is expected to be shipped directly to the Chennai port, while Russia’s Rosneft is already investing in refining infrastructure in India.

In September 2023, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, attending the Eastern Economic Forum, signalled India’s interest in cooperating with Russia on energy and Arctic matters. Another key advantage of the Russian Arctic is the Northern Sea Route (NSR), which is roughly a third shorter than the route via the Indian Ocean and the Suez Canal—offering fast, secure delivery of hydrocarbons to market. This resource base creates the foundation for long-term Russia-India cooperation in the Arctic, with multiplier effects: joint energy projects stimulate NSR development and the socioeconomic growth of coastal regions along the route. India brings substantial financial resources and investment capacity that can support capital-intensive joint Arctic energy projects, while its growing economy offers a stable market for Arctic-extracted hydrocarbons. At the same time, the technological complexity of Arctic operations calls for international cooperation on transport and logistics—jointly developing an effective strategy for the maritime transport of Arctic hydrocarbons that accounts for economic, social, and environmental factors, and minimises impact on a fragile ecosystem. According to available estimates, each job created in the Arctic generates roughly 14 additional jobs in adjacent regions. Also read: BRICS is India’s moment. Its neighbours are watching—and worrying about missing out An Arctic development strategy For India, participation in joint Arctic energy projects also opens opportunities for scientific research in Arctic waters, work on pollution prevention, polar expeditions, and involvement in infrastructure development . It also means a strengthened geopolitical presence in the region and new markets for Indian-made equipment and technology. For Russia, India’s involvement diversifies long-term hydrocarbon exports, strengthens energy diplomacy, and—importantly—increases cargo volumes along the Northern Sea Route, one of Russia’s priority development goals. To deepen this, Russia should draw Indian companies into joint ventures, investment funds, R&D, and equipment supply for Arctic operations, while maintaining a favourable investment climate: tax preferences, priority development zones, and institutional guarantees of transparency and stability for Indian investors. Russia-India cooperation in energy and transport carries real geopolitical weight . T he two countries are forming a new pole of attraction in global energy, demonstrating that effective, partnership-based cooperation between them is possible—and using it as a foundation for a broader Arctic development strategy. Alexey Fadeev is head of the Import Substitution Program at Gazprom Neft and an expert on the Project Office for Arctic Development. Views are personal. (Edited by Prasanna Bachchhav)

Alexey Fadeev is head of the Import Substitution Program at Gazprom Neft and an expert on the Project Office for Arctic Development. Views are personal. (Edited by Prasanna Bachchhav)

For Russia, India’s involvement diversifies long-term hydrocarbon exports, strengthens energy diplomacy, and—importantly—increases cargo volumes along the Northern Sea Route, one of Russia’s priority development goals. To deepen this, Russia should draw Indian companies into joint ventures, investment funds, R&D, and equipment supply for Arctic operations, while maintaining a favourable investment climate: tax preferences, priority development zones, and institutional guarantees of transparency and stability for Indian investors.
