editorials.title: ‘Disappeared’: In Bengal, Muslims picked up from homes in midnight raids, sent to detention centres
editorials.passage:
Parbin Khatun remembers the night of July 29 vividly.

Khatun had returned to her home in Bengal’s Murshidabad district from Kolkata shortly after midnight.

Around 12.30 am, she was in bed, when a group of men knocked on the door of their home in Ramakantapur village.

“They called out my father-in-law’s name,” Khatun said.

When 61-year-old Ibrahim Sheikh opened the door, Khatun said, a group of seven or eight men surrounded him. They were in civilian clothes but Khatun said they appeared to be police officials.

“They demanded to see his documents and so he showed them his Aadhaar and voter cards,” Khatun said. “Then, they asked him, ‘Aapni ki Indian, na Bangaldeshi?’” Are you Indian or Bangladeshi?

Sheikh asserted that he was Indian, not Bangladeshi, Khatun said. But the men said they had information that Sheikh was not an Indian citizen.

They went on to grab Sheikh from behind, Khatun said. As they roughed him up, pinning his hands at the back, he became “very afraid” and “agreed with whatever the police were saying”.

Khatun said the men forcefully took her father-in-law away, alleging that he is a Bangladeshi national. “They did not show us any written document or police complaint against him,” she said.

Khatun said she appealed to the men to consider Sheikh’s age and ill health. “I told them he is sick and weak,” she said. “But they were laughing at him.”

The next day, the family went to the Suti police station with Sheikh’s identity documents – pension papers that showed he was once an employee of the Murshidabad-based company Pataka Bidi, a land title in his name issued in 2017, his voter card, among others.

However, they were not allowed to meet Sheikh.

A day later, the police said he had been sent to a detention centre. “Since then, we have visited Suti police station, the office of the Jangipur superintendent of police and various detention centres,” Khatun said. “But we don’t know where he is. The police have just disappeared him.”

Ibrahim Sheikh is not alone. Scroll’s investigations reveal that since June, at least nine Muslim men and two children have been picked up by the Bengal police from their homes on suspicion of being Bangladeshi nationals and sent to detention centres. All of them except one are from Murshidabad. None was given a chance to prove their citizenship and contest the allegations.

At least four of those detained had cleared the scrutiny of the Election Commission’s special intensive revision of electoral rolls carried out in Bengal recently. Ibrahim Sheikh’s appeal against his exclusion during the SIR is pending at the tribunals set up by the Election Commission.

The detentions have followed a similar pattern. Most detainees were picked from their home in a midnight crackdown – one person while he was sleeping in the verandah outside. Their family members said the police did not produce any warrant or remand order or copy of a first information report to show why they were being taken away. In some cases, the police filed suo motu FIRs weeks after the detentions.

In at least one case, the police’s attempt to expel one of the men was refused by the Border Security Force, police records show.

Since May last year, several Muslim migrant workers from West Bengal have been picked up by police in states ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party. Accused of being Bangladeshis, they have been forcibly pushed out of the country’s borders by the BSF. In at least a couple of cases, they had been brought back on the orders of the Supreme Court.

But this is the first time that Bengali Muslims are facing similar scrutiny and harassment in their own state.

“The scariest thing is that police are randomly picking up people and sending them to detention centres without producing them before the court, which is both illegal and anti-constitutional,” Jakir Hussain, a Murshidabad-based human rights activist associated with the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights, said.

Ibrahim Sheikh’s family has gone to court, seeking redressal.

On August 25, Ibrahim’s 81-year-old mother Hanifa Bewa filed a habeas corpus petition in the Calcutta High Court asking the state to trace Sheikh’s location and produce him in court.

The state government, however, asserted that Hanifa is not the Sheikh’s biological mother.

Sheikh’s lawyer, Md Nur Hossain Zamadar, told Scroll that Hanifa was his maternal aunt, who had adopted him. “This is still an unlawful detention,” he said. “For months now, the family has no idea of his whereabouts. One can’t be detained like this without an arrest memo or an FIR. This is the violation of fundamental rights.”

Zamadar said the family has a land deed document from 1946, which proves they have been living in the country before Independence.

Abhijit Basu Mallick, a senior police official at Suti Police station, rejected allegations by Sheikh’s family members.

“They don’t know the country’s law," Mallick said. “The detention has been done as per the government's executive order. There is no need for an FIR.”

This claim was echoed by Jangipur superintendent of police Surinder Singh. “Everything has been done as per the guidelines,” he said. “The family themselves know that they are Bangladeshis.”

Advocates and activists said the police action remains completely opaque and without legal basis.

“This is not a police state. Detaining any person, treating them as a Bangladeshi, and pushing them back without any investigation is illegal,” said Kirity Roy, activist from Banglar Manabadhikar Suraksha Mancha.

Activists also link the police action to statements made in May by Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari. “Bangladeshi infiltrators detained in the state would be handed over directly to the Border Security Force for deportation instead of being produced before courts,” he said .

Adhikari had clarified that Hindu migrants eligible under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act of 2019 would not be targeted.

Khatun said the police officials who visited her home expressed communal sentiments.

When Khatun tried to dissuade them from taking away Sheikh, the men allegedly told her, “Hindu ra amader buke, Musalman ra amader payer toler.” We will keep Hindus close to our heart, but Muslims have to stay under our feet.

Khatun said they suggested that Hindus had a greater right to stay in India. “They told me: ‘Even if Hindus come from Bangladesh tomorrow, we will make them Indians.’”

Sixty-seven-year-old Jalil Akhtar was sleeping in the verandah of his home in Bahrai village of Uttar Dinajpur district on the midnight of June 19, when the police took him away.

“The police came like thieves in the night and detained him,” his wife Taupha Bibi told Scroll when we visited her one-room hut. “When I woke up and did not see him, I thought he had gone for the morning namaaz. But when he did not return, we went looking for him in the early morning.”

Akhtar’s cousin Matiur Rahman, a retired teacher, found out that he had been taken by personnel from the Dalkhola police station on suspicion of being a Bangladeshi.

The allegation was without basis, Rahman and Taupha said.

Rahman said Akhter’s name had appeared in the electoral roll prepared after the Special Intensive Revision carried out in 2002 as well as 2026. His wife said that they have land documents in the name of Akhter’s great-grandfather.

“When we went to the police station and asked them why he had been picked up, and that his name was cleared in the SIR, they said, ‘You cannot argue with us now. The government has changed, there will be no arguing’," Rahman said.

“What does it mean that the government has changed? It means now we have to face oppression.”

Rahman, who met Akhtar later in Islampur jail, said the police had “kidnapped him”. “He told me that he was threatened into keeping quiet. Everyone would have known if he had screamed and shouted.”

A month after he was taken into custody, an FIR was filed against Akhtar and he was produced before the court.

In these four weeks, the police made at least one attempt to deport him, according to a report filed by the Dalkhola police in the Uttar Dinajpur court on August 1.

Akhtar was kept at a temporary holding centre in Nizampur “and all biometric and deportation formalities were completed”, the report said. He was handed over to the Border Security Force on July 4 and asked to be deported.

But Akhtar insisted he was an Indian citizen. “Consequently, the BSF returned him to police custody,” the Dalkhola police report, seen by Scroll , read.

Having failed to push him out, the police then filed a suo moto case against him under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, accusing him of being a foreigner who had entered the country without a valid passport, travel document, or visa.

Akhtar’s family members say they have submitted land records from 1967, in his father Roshan Ali’s name. But in its report, the police said that Akhtar could not produce any documentary evidence to prove that he was Ali’s son.

The police pointed out that Akhtar could not speak in Bengali, despite claiming to have resided in Uttar Dinajpur for several decades. “Though language by itself cannot determine nationality, the said circumstance has been noted as one of the surrounding facts during enquiry," the police inquiry said

Akhtar’s family speak Surjapuri language, a blend of Hindi, Maithili, and Bengali, spoken mainly in the Bihar-Bengal border region as well as the Islampur subdivision of Uttar Dinajpur district where Akhtar lives. Over three lakh people in Islampur registered Surjapuri as their mother tongue.

Rahman alleged that the police have been picking up Muslims without any basis. “They told me: ‘We have just started. We have 500 names on our list.”

Eleven days after Ibrahim Sheikh was picked up, the Suti police turned up at midnight at a home 3 km away – in Nurpurdiyar village, along the Padma river.

A group of seven or eight police personnel knocked on the door of Jamirul Sheikh at 12.30 am, and asked for his adopted son Abdul Jabbar.

“The police claimed he is Bangladeshi and took him away,” Sheikh said. “But I adopted Jabbar from his maternal grandparents 26 years ago.”

Jabbar’s two sons – eight-year-old Ahad and six-year-old Jiad – were also taken away. His third child, 11-month-old Abdul Halim, is with his wife.

“They have broken up a family,” Jamirul Sheikh said.

The police officials asked Sheikh to visit the police station with Jabbar’s documents. “They said we will release him. But the next day, they did not even allow us to meet him.”

Instead, the police officials showed Sheikh a Bangladeshi birth certificate issued in 2022, saying Jabbar was a Bangladeshi. “This is a fake document,” Sheikh said.

He cited the several documents that Jabbar has – an Indian passport, a birth certificate issued by the sub-registrar of Nupur gram panchayat and a voter card. Scroll has seen the documents.

Jabbar voted in the last Assembly elections after having been included in the electoral rolls after the special intensive revision or SIR in Bengal.

“He is Indian and his mother is also Indian,” Jamirul told Scroll . “We adopted him after her mother left the country with his father, who is from Bangladesh.”

In the 1990s, marriages between families on either side of the border were common as there was no fencing, said Jakir Hossain, the Murshidabad-based activist.

Jabbar was born in 1990. Under the Citizenship Amendment Act, a person born in India after 1950 and before 2003 is an Indian citizen if one of his or her parents is Indian – and if the other is not an illegal migrant.

Jamirul said Jabbar grew up at his nana nani’s home in Lakhipur gram panchayat till the age of eight. “He has been with us for the last 26 years,” he said. “We were not even given a chance to prove he is Indian.”

A few days after his detention, Jabbar's 26-year-old wife Jumman Bibi was admitted to a hospital in Jangipur.

"She was admitted after she had seizures and lost consciousness,” her brother Nobinul Hoque said. “She keeps fainting. Her two sons are missing."

Jumman told Scroll that the police had told her that Jabbar and her children had been pushed into Bangladesh. “We last spoke with him on August 28 when he was in the Ahiran detention centre.”

On June 14, Sahin Sheikh, a 28-year-old resident of Budher Kismat village, was picked up in a midnight raid by the Murshidabad police.

“When we opened the door, the police started to question Sahin, asking him about his father’s and grandfather’s names. They claimed he was a Bangladeshi national,” his wife Amina Khatun said.

“My husband said he was born here and has lived here all his life,” she said. When she submitted documents to the police station, including a land deed from 2003, and a ration card issued by the state government, the police refused to accept them.

Sahin Sheikh was not included in the voter roll after the SIR this year, but he has appealed the exclusion in the appellate tribunals set up by the EC.

Sheikh was moved to the Lalgola detention centre. Since then, Amina said, the police made attempts to push him into Bangladesh.

As in Akhtar’s case, the police waited several weeks to file a case against Sahin Sheikh.

His advocate Mohammed Abu Raihain told Scroll that the police filed a suo moto FIR 20 days later, on July 6, after having failed to push him into Bangladesh.

“This is completely illegal,” he said. “The police FIR says they got information from a source that he is a Bangladeshi.”

According to the suo moto FIR seen by Scroll , the police alleged that during the search of his bag, a photocopy of a birth certificate from Bangladesh was recovered, indicating his Bangladeshi origin. “But this document has not been proved as authentic,” Raihan said.

Raihan claimed the whole case is based on “lies and fabrication” as police have not verified the birth certificate and other documents. “I asked the courts to verify Sahin’s voter card, panchayat certificate, school certificate and land documents. Let the Election Commission and Murshidabad district administration verify and say whether these are fake documents or not.”

Murshidabad-based advocate Sahin Mandal said the police action in several such cases violated all constitutional provisions. “At the direction of the current government, the police are picking up whoever they want.”

Jibon Sheikh, one of Sahin’s clients, was taken away on the night of June 26 by the Murshidabad police. “He has all the documents, from a voter card to school certificate but the police refused to accept them,” Sahin said. “He has voted in the recent assembly elections after having been included in the SIR.”

Since then, his 27-year-old wife Farida Bibi has been trying to release him from Lalgola holding centre, a detention centre. “He even has an identity card issued by the Bengal government stating he is a fish trader. They still took him,” Farida said.

In the last three months, Farida said, she has exhausted her savings trying to keep the home running. The couple has three children, the oldest is 13.

Advocate Selim Sheikh, who is among the lawyers representing Sheikh, told Scroll that even after more than two months no FIR copy or any other order was given to the family which is violating the constitutional provision. “We are moving Calcutta High Court next week challenging his detention,” Selim said.

editorials.title: In Pune, noise pollution debate raises the pitch ahead of Ganesh festival
editorials.passage:
When 37-year-old Pune resident Vidyanand Bapat last month publicly criticised the noise and traffic obstructions during the Ganesh festival, he struck a raw nerve.

Ever since freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak transformed the Ganeshotsav into a public celebration in 1893 to circumvent a colonial ban on assembly, it has become Pune’s signature event.

During the ten-day festival honouring the birth of the elephant-headed deity, Pune fills up with elaborate pandals housing Ganesh idols. Dhol tasha drum groups parade through the streets. There are plays about the 17th-century warrior king Shivaji. Religious songs and prayers echo from stacks of loudspeakers.

At a preparatory meet for Ganeshotsav called by the Pune Municipal Corporation on August 24, Bapat spoke angrily about how the music played by loudspeakers is a burden for residents. “The loudspeakers on stands play all through the 10 days,” he said. “On the last two days, they are played 24 hours.”

He caused a furore. Other participants tried to shout him down. In videos, some can be heard telling him to get out of Pune if he has a problem. The police had to escort Bapat out of the meeting.

Bapat – a Brahmin who speaks in chaste Marathi, given to quoting Sanskrit texts – has become the unlikely spokesperson for longstanding grievances about noise pollution during the festival.

After all, the Ganesh celebrations in Pune have been definitively shaped by the cultural sensibilities of Brahmins and other upper-caste groups , scholars note.

However, over the decades, its contours have widened to make it more inclusive of other caste groups and of women . For instance, dhol tasha pathaks, or groups, prominently feature women. This has given the festival a mass appeal.

The popularity of the festival, coupled with a growing assertion of the Hindu identity in recent years, could explain why some are outraged by Bapat’s suggested restrictions on Ganeshotsav, scholars say

Bapat has demanded that DJs and loudspeakers be banned, that dhol tasha performances be moved to indoor auditoriums and that pandals be constructed only on designated grounds.

The notion that Bapat’s assertions were not aimed a solving a civic problem but an attack on religion was evident on September 3, as he was being interviewed on the street by a television journalist. Suddenly, a man stepped up and slapped him, shouting abuses at Bapat for “speaking against Ganpati”.

Others share this view. Chinmay Abhyankar, the president of Khalkar Jog Mitra Mandal was also sceptical of Bapat’s campaign.

Mitra mandals or “organisations of friends”, such as the one that Abhyankar heads, consists of volunteers from a neighbourhood and are central to organising the festival. There are an estimated 2,000 or more such groups in Pune.

Abhyankar conceded that Bapat’s concerns about loud DJs and traffic congestion are valid but expressed doubts about the activist’s motives. “By opposing everything means that his agenda is questionable,” Abhyankar declared. “By Bappa’s grace, he will not succeed.” In Marathi, “Bappa” is a term of endearment for the deity Ganesh.

Also dismissive of the criticism about noise was 33-year-old Jugal Chandan of the Shree Krishna Mandal Trust in the Deccan Gymkhana area. He said the mandal with which he is associated is nearly nine decades old and that one person should not try to disrupt this long tradition.

“Entertainment and festivals go hand in hand,” Chandan said. “You can’t say ‘celebrate quietly’. Be it any religion.”

Chandan said these concerns should have been raised earlier instead of this close to the festival, when people’s time and money is at stake. The first day of Ganesh Chaturthi is September 14.

As the debate gathered steam, Pune Police Commissioner Amitesh Kumar Police on September 4 said that plasma speakers and pressure-mids , which amplify sound, and laser lights had been banned.

At a meeting, mandals agreed to a limit of four top speakers and four base speakers .

Even so, on September 6, about 1,000 citizens marched though the city under the banner of the “ Punekars Against Loudspeakers Forum ” seeking a ban on “DJ” sound systems.

Krunnal Gharre, an advocate who was affiliated with the city’s Aam Aadmi Party unit, said that despite several Supreme Court, High Court and National Green Tribunal judgements on noise, “there is no compliance from the mandals”.

The claim by members of mandals that the issue had been raised too close to the festival is irrelevant, said Gharre. He noted that India has had noise pollution rules since 2000 and that the National Green Tribunal had issued orders on controlling noise during Ganeshotsav in Pune in 2024.

The state pollution control board had told the tribunal that sound levels in Pune on peak days of the festival were consistently above 90 decibels – a dangerous level that could damage hearing over time.

Despite the disruptions, Gharre conceded that since festivals involve acute social sensitivities, it is essential to find the middle ground. “You enjoy your sound but that sound should not enter someone else’s home and cause them discomfort,” Gharre said. “I mean, window glasses breaking [from the vibrations caused by loud sound] and all that is too much.”

Members of Ganesh mandals, on their part, say they are well aware of the sound limits and insist that they follow the rules.

But Bapat’s demand that the festival be moved out of city limits is not practical, said Abhayankar. “Our people and society are here,” he said. “We can’t change everything just because one person is unhappy and venting his frustrations on the Ganeshotsav.”

Amar Harish Supekar, who has been associated with the Samarth Pratisthan dhol tasha pathak for 20 years, said that the festival serves an essential function: it unites society at a time when people are disconnected and isolated.

Supekar, who works as a researcher, said that most Pune residents enjoy dhol tasha performances. “It is a distributed, dispersed sound and hence causes less noise,” he claimed.

Behind Supekar, youngsters sat watching a dhol tasha pathak practice at a spot by the Mutha river. After complaints about noise, many pathaks shifted their practice sessions away from residential areas to open grounds or roads by the river.

He dismissed suggestions that dhol tasha performances should be restricted to closed auditoriums. “This is the city’s and the whole state’s festival,” Supekar said. “How can it be celebrated in an auditorium?”

An academic who has researched religion and culture in Pune’s middle-class said Bapat’s views have trapped members of the city’s upper castes in a bind.

“They actually want to support him on noise pollution,” said the academic, but they feel defensive because Ganeshotsav is seen as a marker of identity – a symbol of “our” festival and “our” religion.

Hindu majoritarianism has reshaped Indian society, said the academic. As the texture of society changes, many upper-caste Pune residents feel a false sense of anxiety about Hindu culture being under threat, said the academic. They feel that “even if Bapat is rational and correct, it is a question of life and death, of existence and identity”.

The mandals and dhol tasha pathaks, the academics noted, are institutions that help consolidate this fragmenting sense of community.

But opposition to Bapat’s campaign is more widespread. As the festival grew to include expressions by groups beyond the dominant castes, it gave more groups “the sense of being able to claim and be part of a culture which was not available to them earlier”, said the academic.

As a consequence, subscribing to Bapat’s views could be perceived as a decision “not to assert your identity in public as Hindu”.

The academic concluded: “To view festivals with the objectivity and rationality of Bapat is a novelty right now – even though there is nothing novel about what Bapat is saying.”

The voice in the din: Why Vidyanand Bapat is making noise about noise

editorials.title: Food history: How the French ‘stole’ and transplanted cloves in their colonies in the 18th century
editorials.passage:
Nations that controlled islands where spices were grown were extremely protective of their crops. The Dutch, above all, were highly sensitive about protection. To stop their nutmeg from being reseeded, they covered this export crop with lime. The Dutch also set their clove groves on fire both to control the market and to keep others from getting a new crop from the plants. During the Age of Exploration and into the 19th century, there were many attempts by European nations to steal spice seeds or plants. In the last quarter of the 18th century, a French adventurer, Pierre Poivre (Peter Pepper), was successful. Poivre had spent a great deal of time in Asia as a young man, doing various types of work for the French. At different times he was a prisoner of the Dutch, and he lost an arm when his ship was taken by the British near the Straits of Malacca. He was especially interested in botany and decided to try to bring tropical plants into French hands. On a few occasions he attempted to transplant clove and nutmeg onto French soil, but the seedlings always died. He eventually settled on Mauritius, in the south-west Indian Ocean just east of Madagascar. Working there as a French political official, he built a house and started a garden of tropical plants on the island. He soon returned to the Moluccas in search of spices and was lucky to run across a disenchanted Dutchman who directed him to an island where he could obtain a preponderance of nutmeg and clove seedlings from natives who were secretly growing and hiding them from the Dutch. So the aptly named Frenchman was able to bring a large quantity of seedlings back to Mauritius to his garden.

Trade between Africa and the Arab world had existed for centuries. There were trade connections between Africa, India and Asia involving slaves, gold and ivory. The original inhabitants of Zanzibar were Hadimu, Tumbatu and Pemba peoples, who had been drawn out from interior Africa by the fresh water and fertile soil of the large island off East Africa. In the late tenth century, Persians came to the island, settled there briefly, and then left to be replaced by Arabs from Oman. Zanzibar became a focal point for commerce, since it served as an entry point in East Africa for trade links with the interior. Prior to Portuguese exploration of the East African coast, many Indians from South Asia migrated to Zanzibar, where they served as shopkeepers, traders and skilled workers. The Portuguese briefly ruled Zanzibar until 1550, when they were ousted by the Sultan of Oman. For a few centuries, Zanzibar was a corner of a global trade network where Africans, Arabs, Chinese, Europeans, Indians and Persians met.

The British became involved with Zanzibar in the late 18th century and throughout the 19th century. The public in Great Britain increased its interest in Zanzibar because the explorers Burton, David Livingstone and John Speke launched their expeditions there. The British signed treaties with the sultan to protect Zanzibar in exchange for Omani support against the French. Britain had outlawed slavery in 1807 and made many attempts to influence the Sultan of Zanzibar to do the same. Agreements were signed to eliminate slavery in the 1870s, but progress was slow. Zanzibar was an increasingly important trading centre, and from the 1820s onwards, American, German and British trading ships had established Zanzibar as a major port.

Excerpted with permission from Spices: A Global History, Fred Czarra, Pan Macmillan India.

editorials.title: Brics Summit: A stern rebuke to Trump’s unilateralism and expansion of India’s strategic space
editorials.passage:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi should consider sending a ‘thank you’ note to Donald Trump. The success of the 18th edition of the Brics summit under India’s chairship owes a lot to his antics.

While evaluating the event, I can’t help but think about the way the Western media has reacted to it. Ignoring the summit for the most part bar perfunctory reporting from a povertarian lens (e.g., consider this photo carried by The New York Times as a defining image from the Brics Summit, the dominant narrative nevertheless has been a binary between whether the members are ‘conspiring’ to dethrone the US dollar or failing to do so.

Perhaps it’s the inherent solipsism that compels the West to perceive the world as a binary between those ‘with us’ and those ‘against us’. I don’t know. What I do know is that Trump’s aggressive unilateralism, hyper-transactionalist foreign policy, unrestrained militarism, bullying of allies and partners, abusive communication style and economic protectionism have acted as a binding force for Brics members to shelve their internal differences and project an image of unity and resolve.

In a fragmented landscape that defines the anxious space between the decline of a hegemon and the rise of a challenger, the 18th edition in New Delhi achieved a result of great consequence. Countries with profound internal conflicts and diverse interests sat across a table and were able to reach a consensus.

Consensus is not necessarily unanimity. A document forged out of consensus involving give and take from all sides does not need to be unanimous. The fact that India managed to thrash out the joint statement at all despite some members currently navigating severe bilateral tension sends a clear message across the world about the structural effectiveness of the Brics platform.

Without explicitly naming the United States, the summit sent a clear, unified message to the Trump administration — that the Global South will not be a passive recipient of economic coercion, nor will it allow its developmental trajectories to be derailed by the tariff wars and unilateral sanctions.

As paragraph 22 from the New Delhi Declaration pointed out, “We condemn the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law, and reiterate that such measures, inter alia in the form of unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have far-reaching negative implications for the human rights, including the rights to development, health and food security, of the general population of targeted states, disproportionally affecting the poor and people in vulnerable situations, deepening the digital divide and exacerbating environmental challenges.”

The declaration was particularly vocal regarding global trade and economic architecture. It voiced “serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules”.

The language referenced the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to international trade, including the introduction of so-called ‘reciprocal tariffs’. The communique called for the immediate restoration of a “fully functioning, two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism,” targeting the US policy of blocking appointments to the WTO’s Appellate Body, which has paralysed the institution.

On the escalating conflict in West Asia, the declaration voiced “serious concern” over attacks on civilian infrastructure and “peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the IAEA”. This was a clear condemnation of actions taken during the recent escalations in West Asia, emphasizing that such strikes violate international law and IAEA resolutions. It amounts to a blunt rebuke of the US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. By framing these strikes as violations of international law, the operations are termed ‘illegal aggression’.

The fact that India is a signatory to a document that criticises the actions of US and Israel in such terms may not necessarily mean that New Delhi was fully behind the language. It is, however, the hallmark of a consensus document where compromises have to be made. What India seems to have achieved in return is quite extraordinary.

Paragraph 40 states that Brics members “express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured. We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.”

It is worth noting that instead of “Pahalgam”, the text situates the Pakistan-sponsored terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir. This adds a layer of validation to Jammu and Kashmir as India’s sovereign space and leaves little space for Pakistan to manoeuvre. China’s policy has always been to refer to Jammu and Kashmir as “disputed” in line with Pakistan’s narrative. For the Chinese to concede that Jammu and Kashmir belongs to India in a signed document is a substantial achievement of Indian diplomacy.

Beyond geopolitical posturing, the summit pushed towards frameworks for resilient global supply chains and cross-border payment integration.

Paragraph 90 provides an interesting insight into the diversity of opinion among members of a common payment mechanism beyond the overarching need for building a resilient architecture that may shield members from America’s weaponisation of the dollar or the SWIFT banking system.

The text stressed on “exploring pragmatic solutions for efficient cross-border payment mechanisms”, “while respecting national priorities and acknowledging that there is no one-size-fits-all approach.” There are clearly two sets of opinion on this. While members such as Russia, China and Iran want an alternative to the Western financial architecture dominated by the US, for India, the aim is a more limited one – a bilateral payment mechanism through local currencies.

India’s nuanced position evolves from its need to stay within the America-led financial ecosystem while ensuring that it retains options when things go south.

Evidently, if it needed to be reinforced, the summit proved again that New Delhi is a moderating force within the platform. It does not want to create an anti-West bloc, push the global architecture towards an antagonistic environment, or replace a US-led order with a China-led one.

India’s idea within the Brics platform is to foster greater cooperation among members and limit the deleterious impact of a declining hegemon’s unpredictable actions. New Delhi also seeks to reform legacy Bretton Woods Institutions “to make them more agile, effective, credible, inclusive, fit for purpose, unbiased, accountable, and representative, to enhance their legitimacy” and to make their governance structure amenable to “transformation of the global economy since their establishment.”

But if that can’t be done within the existing global order, in India’s vision, Brics should prepare options for members to eventually do so.

To my mind, the summit expanded the space for India to exercise its strategic autonomy. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is the only world leader who may share embraces with both Benjamin Netanyahu and Masoud Pezeshkian. The image of Prime Minister Modi clasping the hands of the Iranian president will remain the defining image of the summit.

The fact that India can utilise the Brics framework to engage with multiple global powers simultaneously ensures New Delhi evaluates global partnerships based strictly on its own developmental needs and security interests.

From New Delhi’s standpoint, the summit functioned as a calculated mechanism to buffer the Indian economy against global unpredictability. By inching towards energy security cooperation and an alternative financial routing system within the Brics network, New Delhi is building systemic shock absorbers that may allow for parallel tracks to maintain trade and commerce.

More to the point, India executed this hedging strategy while safeguarding its access to and integration with Western markets, capital and technology. Navigating the Brics framework did not require India to pivot away from the US or Europe.

India’s demonstrated capacity to manage competing interests and moderate the Global South enhances its indispensable value to Western and non-Western partners. India showed that it may engage robustly with non-Western powers while avoiding Cold War-style bloc politics. The summit validated India’s capacity to lead in a volatile era, securing its own economic future while championing a more equitable, cooperative global order.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Pezeshkian at Brics: India’s diplomacy without divides
editorials.passage:
India very successfully hosted the 18th Brics Summit with leaders from eleven member countries and ten partner countries as well as invitees from international organisations, including the UNSG. All major leaders, especially President Putin, President Xi Jinping and President Ramaphosa, attended the summit and shared their vision. Brazilian President Lula could not attend, being busy with his own elections, where US influence might work against him. The deliberations by the full house, combined with assiduous and smart diplomacy of Indian negotiators and the firm leadership of Prime Minister yielded the most comprehensive, principled, practical and Global South-oriented Brics ‘New Delhi Declaration’ by consensus.

This was a remarkable feat indeed, given the ongoing regional conflict, divergences and rivalries between Iran, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia. There is no doubt that Prime Minister Modi’s meetings with Dr Pezeshkian and the UAE Crown Prince may have facilitated bridging of differences to some extent. Earlier, during the Foreign Ministers’ meeting, due to a lack of consensus, a chair’s statement had to be issued. Bridging the divides is what India is adept, as it showed during the G20 Summit in 2023.

While the presence of all leaders was significant and important one could discern the special public and media attention that the Iranian President, Dr Masoud Pezeshkian, received. On the bilateral front as well, his picture with Prime Minister Modi walking hand in hand along with President Putin conveyed a special meaning and comfort. This was his first visit to India since taking over, even though both leaders have spoken on several occasions, especially since the war began. Incidentally, Dr Jaishankar was the first foreign dignitary to call on Dr Pezeshkian before he took over. In his interview with Geeta Mohan of India Today he clearly spoke of his relationship with Prime Minister Modi and India which is improving on a daily basis while attributing historic, civilizational and strategic ties between the two Asian powers. He was also the only leader to have been received by President Murmu. He was accompanied by his family members and his daughter was seen shopping at the Bharat Mandapam.

This was the second meeting between Prime Minister Modi and President Pezeshkian in less than two weeks after the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Bishkek summit when the regional situation was discussed. The bilateral meeting this time also dealt with all key issues of mutual concern including in the context of Brics. The ending of this war and all wars is a priority, and India is not hesitating to contribute to de-escalation to the extent possible. The Ministry of External Affairs readout of the bilateral meeting emphasised, “The two leaders exchanged views on recent developments in West Asia. Prime Minister reiterated India’s consistent position that all issues must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy. He also underscored the need for continued efforts to ensure lasting peace and stability in the region, safeguarding freedom of navigation and commerce, and the safety and well-being of seafarers.” Since Indian seafarers and trade and energy security have been greatly impacted by the war and closure of Strait of Hormuz, Prime Minister Modi in his opening remarks at Brics proposed the establishment of a ‘Seafarers Emergency Support Network’. This network could connect the maritime authorities and missions of the countries concerned. It could facilitate distress alerts, medical assistance, communication with families, and support for evacuation. “India is becoming a global solution hub”, he added.

The Iranian President used his visit and several interactions including with the media and on the Brics platform to pinpoint the unjustified US and Israeli aggression against his country. He condemned US and Israeli attacks by saying, “Today, Iran has been able to successfully stand against Israel and the United States at the same time; they want to bully us, and we do not want to be bullied. We never kneel down before them. If they push us, we push back. They claim that they are advocates of human rights. In truth, they are the devils who are the true terrorists, because they killed 168 schoolchildren in one instant, thanks to their modern technologies.”

Taking full advantage of a powerful platform, addressing the Leaders' Session of the Brics Business Forum, Pezeshkian highlighted the tough times through which the global economy is currently passing due to geopolitics, disruption of supply chains, and the rising influence of economics as a tool of politics. Urging diversification of trade partners, sources of financing and payment channels, he called for greater use of national currencies in intra-Brics trade comparing “Economic security is inseparable from national and regional security”. Prior to the Summit, he set the tone that the goal of Brics was to confront unilateralism and reduce dependence on dominant global financial systems. While sending a message to Tel Aviv and Washington that “We will not surrender to oppression. We will not be bullied, and if they push, we will push them back”, he also offered Iran’s potential as a bridge for Brics energy, food and transport supply chains referring to its geography and energy resources. Ironically that bridge is broken due to war and closure of Hormuz and threats of closure of Bab-el-Mandeb the key arteries of trade and energy supplies.

He also had several bilaterals, but the most important one in the context of the ongoing conflict was with the UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled – the highest-level interaction since the war began. Although Pezeshkian claimed that Iran was committed to peaceful coexistence in the Gulf, he added that they have no problem with the UAE but object the presence of US and Israeli bases. The Gulf country has been the most hit and impacted and became collateral damage, perhaps also due to its close relationship with US and Israel. However, in recent times they have condemned the actions of Israel in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and the West Bank, joining other Islamic countries.  Hence, the meeting was significant, especially as Oman has pioneered a meeting between the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Iran to discuss navigation and other issues on September 14. Credit for this highest-level meeting between the two current adversaries does go to Prime Minister Modi’s personalised diplomacy.

What Prime Minister Modi said at G7 in France applies ipso facto to Brics and the rest of the international community and organisations: partnerships can succeed only when they are built on trust. Today, the most strategic asset is not minerals, technology, or markets — it is mutual trust.

How do you turn the pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership? That is the key question.

(Anil Trigunayat is a former Indian ambassador to Jordan, Libya and Malta and a distinguished fellow and head of the West Asia Experts Group at the prestigious Vivekananda International Foundation. He is also a Distinguished Fellow at the oldest Indian think tank, the United Services Institution of India. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Yemen’s war has just become everyone’s problem
editorials.passage:
For anyone trying to understand Yemen, the first difficulty is identifying who is fighting whom. Strip away the complications and the picture becomes easier. On one side are the Houthis, formally Ansar Allah, a Zaydi Shia movement which controls Yemen's capital, Sana'a, and much of the north and west. Iran has supported it with weapons, technology, training and advice, although the Houthis have their own Yemeni identity, interests and ambitions.

Against them stands Yemen's internationally recognised government, backed principally by Saudi Arabia. But this side has never been a single coherent force. It includes different military formations, tribal groups and political interests. The Southern Transitional Council (STC), supported by the UAE and seeking an independent southern Yemen, is also strongly anti-Houthi. Tariq Saleh's National Resistance Forces, operating along the Red Sea coast, are another important component.

This fragmentation matters because the Houthis have something their opponents have struggled to achieve: unity of command and purpose.
Why the Latest Offensive Matters
The Houthis seized Sana’a in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily the following year, leading a coalition intended to restore the recognised government. Years of air strikes inflicted enormous damage but failed to dislodge the Houthis. A fragile truce eventually reduced the fighting without settling the conflict. That uneasy situation has now broken down dramatically.

In a lightning offensive, Houthi forces have swept southwards along Yemen's Red Sea coast, capturing the historic port of Mocha and reaching Perim, or Mayun, Island in the middle of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are attempting to recover lost ground.

Bab al-Mandab is no obscure geographical feature. Only about 29 km wide at its narrowest, it is the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Around 7 per cent of global petroleum supplies normally pass through it. Disruption forces shipping around the Cape of Good Hope, adding time and cost.

Suddenly, therefore, a Yemeni civil war has become everyone's problem.
Iran and the Two Straits
The timing makes the Houthi advance particularly significant.

Iran’s confrontation with the US has already severely disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global oil supplies passed before the current war. Saudi Arabia consequently became increasingly dependent upon its East-West pipeline to move oil to Red Sea ports.

That pipeline has now itself come under drone attack and was temporarily shut. Meanwhile, an Iranian partner has reached Bab el-Mandeb at the other end of the Arabian Peninsula.

The strategic implication is straightforward. Iran does not need physically to control both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. It needs sufficient capability to make both unsafe.

That gives Tehran leverage disproportionate to its conventional military strength.

It also says something about the much-discussed decline of Iran's "Axis of Resistance". Hamas and Hezbollah have suffered grievously, and Iran itself has absorbed enormous punishment. Yet networks do not have to survive everywhere equally. The Houthis have emerged as perhaps the most resilient element of this ecosystem. Geography makes them especially valuable.
America’s Uncomfortable Choice
The US now confronts an unenviable choice. It cannot easily accept Houthi domination of Bab al-Mandab. Freedom of navigation, energy supplies and the credibility of American security arrangements are involved. Yet another major campaign against the Houthis would consume aircraft, ships, intelligence assets and precious air-defence munitions while Washington is already engaged against Iran.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has reportedly sought American military assistance. Washington has so far declined direct intervention while offering intelligence support.

There is good reason for caution. The Houthis survived years of Saudi-led air attacks and subsequent American strikes. They have learnt, dispersed and adapted.

This is also where the military lesson becomes important. Non-contact warfare can destroy infrastructure, launchers and command centres. It cannot by itself permanently secure territory. The Houthis have understood this well. They combine missiles and drones with organised fighters who ultimately move forward and occupy ground.
Mecca Accord Faces Its First Test
For India, there is another dimension worth watching. Only last month Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. Its most striking provision was the principle that an attack upon one would be treated as an attack upon all (much like NATO Article 5). That sounded formidable on paper. Yemen may now provide an unexpectedly early test of what it actually means.

Saudi Arabia is being attacked by Houthi missiles and drones. Pakistan has strongly condemned the attacks and reaffirmed its commitment to the Mecca agreement. Yet Islamabad has also clarified that no military response under the pact has so far been discussed. That distinction is important.

Defence agreements acquire credibility not at signing ceremonies but when one member actually comes under attack. Will Pakistan and Turkey provide intelligence, air defence, naval support, weapons or forces? Or will collective defence essentially mean diplomatic solidarity unless the threat becomes existential?

There is another complication. The three partners do not share identical security priorities. Saudi Arabia’s immediate threat now comes from Iran-aligned forces. Pakistan remains primarily concerned with India and Afghanistan, while Turkey has its own strategic priorities.

India therefore has reason to watch closely. The issue is not whether the Mecca Accord is directed at India. It is whether the agreement is evolving into a genuine military alliance with operational obligations, or remains essentially a framework for political and strategic coordination.

Yemen may provide the first answer.
The Larger Lesson
There is irony in what is unfolding. The Houthis were once the insurgents whom a powerful Saudi-led coalition expected to defeat. More than a decade later, they are threatening one of the world's great maritime chokepoints and forcing Washington, Riyadh, Islamabad and Ankara to reconsider their options.

This does not mean the Houthis have won Yemen. Holding newly captured territory may prove harder than seizing it, and Saudi-backed forces are already responding.

But the strategic map has changed, bringing greater turbulence. Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab can no longer be viewed as separate waterways belonging to separate crises. Iran sits beside one. Its most resilient regional partner now threatens the other. All others seem pushed onto the defensive.

That is why Yemen’s war has suddenly become everyone’s problem.

(The author is Governor of Bihar, former Member of NDMA and former Commander of India’s Srinagar-based Chinar Corps. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Deal-Maker Modi? Decoding NYT's Sudden Praise for India's Foreign Policy
editorials.passage: In an article late August, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s foreign policy received a thumbs up from a very prominent US newspaper which has usually been a harsh critic of his governance record. The newspaper reported that faced with US President Donald Trump’s erratic conduct, especially on trade and tariffs, Modi, showing remarkable energy, undertook travels to many countries to stitch ‘deals’.  Equally, many countries’ leaders visited India to “secure access to the world's fastest growing large economy”.The fact that India was able to successfully steer and find common ground during the BRICS Delhi Summit to issue a Declaration would have been in keeping with the report’s thrust. The newspaper’s write-up would have been appreciated by the Modi government especially because its relations with this newspaper have been largely acrimonious.In 2019, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, referring to its criticism, asserted that India’s reputation was not decided by a newspaper in New York.In a World of Regime Complexity, What Does India Want From BRICS?How should the newspaper’s comments be interpreted, especially as the newspaper is a harsh critic of the Trump administration? Does it reflect the fear, in some US circles, that Trump’s pressures and erratic conduct is endangering the India-US relationship whose upward trajectory has enjoyed wide bipartisan support for two decades?This section feels that instead of further cementing India-US ties, Modi is being forced to look to fostering or strengthening partnerships with other countries, many of whom have been stung by Trump’s policies and actions too.It does so because US analysts would have particularly noted Modi’s outreach to Europe, which has been reciprocated. This is despite Trump’s tantrums and invective against Europe transatlantic ties remain very  consequential in world trade, technology transfers, and capital movement. This is not likely to change. This stated, it is necessary to examine if Modi has undertaken more foreign travels over the last two years than he did since becoming PM in 2014. Except for the COVID-19 pandemic years, Modi maintained a hectic pace of foreign travel for bilateral and multilateral visits. The number of the trips since 2025 has not shown a dramatic increase.   India-US Trade Deal: Why Agriculture Holds the Real LeverageIndia traditionally has had a trade surplus with the US. In financial year 2025-26, India surplus was $33.8 billion in merchandise trade. In addition, in the services sector, the surplus was over $4 billion. The US market in goods and services is exceedingly important for India. Both were deeply disturbed by Trump’s imposition of tariffs on Indian goods last year—and his visa policies that restricted the activities of the Indian tech companies. Both countries are now in the midst of working on a trade deal.BRICS Expansion Tests India's Balancing Act Between China, Russia and the WestOn 9 September, India’s Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal was quoted in the press as saying, “The India-US Trade Pact is more or less finalised, with only a few issues being discussed by the two sides, and it will be signed at the appropriate time”. Such positive noises are being made by Delhi and Washington for some months. It is known that Trump wants India to open up sensitive areas in the agriculture sector—and that will be politically costly for Modi. Hence, despite these soothing sounds, it is only when the trade pact is inked and ratified that there will be some certainty for Indian exporters. The word ‘some’ is used deliberately because Trump has a history of tearing up bilateral and multilateral agreements. Hence, even with a pact, there will not be any complete certainty as long as Trump remains in office. In these circumstances, it was prudent for Modi to spread India’s trading and services options—as well as to make it clear that India will protect its energy security in a manner which was advantageous to it.Hence, the continuance of buying Russian oil was correct—and it was good that Modi defied the American and European pressures on this account. The problem, however, is that there are no markets which can really replace the US market for India’s goods and services sectors. That can be seen in the fact that in merchandise exports, India has a trade surplus with only six of its 25 leading trading partners—and that its merchandise deficit is over $333 billion.Admittedly, a lot of this deficit is because of imports of hydrocarbons but the elephant in the room is China, with which India’s trade deficit has reached $112 billion despite all of Modi’s efforts at atmanirbharta (self reliance). There are no prospects of this changing soon. Thus, the purple prose of the Ministry of Commerce’s statement some months ago is exaggerated.The statement noted, “These agreements are for farmers… They are for entrepreneurs, women-led MSMEs exporting garments, leather and handicrafts with new competitiveness. They are for talent… IT professionals, chefs, yoga instructors who now have choices and clear mobility pathways to work, to study, and to build futures supported by post-study work visas, mobility, and social security relief. They are for organic products and traditional wellness systems of AYUSH. They are for digital services, powering the worlds’ AI. They are for catalysing investments and making our FTA partners, our stakeholders”. Subhash Garg Writes: Centre's FAQs on GDP Revision Lack Crucial Supporting DataApart from trade, there is also an enormous challenge that India faces because of the breathtakingly rapid advance of the current fourth industrial revolution encompassing AI and robotics. In these areas, the leading countries are the US and China. European states, Japan, and South Korea are puny players in the AI field. Cutting-edge work that will define many aspects of human life is taking place only in the US and China. Unfortunately, unlike the third industrial revolution encompassing IT and computers—when India could and did play a role, now it will find it very difficult to do so.The deals being made by Modi will not assist in this process because the partner-countries of these deals cannot assist in the AI field. This part has been missed by the US newspaper article altogether. The international order is in a churn. The middle powers, especially those with nuclear weapons, may be able to defend themselves especially when faced with existential crises. But, for real progress, the path lies through progress in cutting-edge technology in AI.Not all the attempts at reaching out to the world can help in this process. Neither will multilateral documents of summits such as BRICS address the situation except marginally.The only path lies through a commitment of becoming a truly scientific and technological power. Contrary to what the article suggests, the path to that does not lie through trade deals and opening up ties with other states. (The writer is a former Secretary [West], Ministry of External Affairs. He can be reached @VivekKatju. This is an opinion piece, and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)To Win in the Kingdom of AI, India Must Stop Celebrating Data Centres

editorials.title: India Leaps on Transparency Index: Publishes Raw GDP Data, Does Full VVPAT Count
editorials.passage:
Transparency is the glitziest ornament of a credible democracy. But an insecure state often buries that ornament in an abyss of extraneous, obfuscating details.  In India, we’ve confronted incredibly sticky questions around two population-scale processes—ie, how we estimate our GDP and count votes. Because these processes impact the lives of 1.4 billion citizens—ie, they are not small, isolated, or one-off problems, but gigantic exercises recurring at “population scale”—it’s critical to be, and to be SEEN, as pristine, beyond reproach. It’s the “Caesar’s wife moment” for our eight-decade-young democracy.     Subhash Garg Writes: Centre's FAQs on GDP Revision Lack Crucial Supporting DataLet’s tackle GDP first. We surprised the world with a strong upswing, ie real GDP growth of 7.8 percent in the first quarter of the current year. Despite two global wars, supply shocks, stinging inflation, and a plummeting rupee and capital markets, our economy was in the pink of health. There was a significant caveat—this estimate was based on a new methodology.  Independent experts were quick to pick two “tweaks” which, prima facie, required transparent detailing.  First, last year’s GDP at current prices was slashed by over Rs 12 trillion, or almost four percent. The government defended, asserting it was caused by the new methodology. Fair enough. Yet experts did not relent. Experts: “Sir, you have all the information, please blow up this Rs 12 trillion shrinkage into components—like a punching error, or over-estimation cleaned up by new data, or other reasons.” State (air of injured innocence): “This is a much more credible, scientific model. The World Bank and IMF are applauding. Why are you attacking us?”.  Experts (nonplussed): “Who is attacking the new methodology? We too are applauding, it’s the correct way forward. But yes, we are asking you to reconcile this outlandish Rs 12 trillion number, or give us the raw data, and Claude will do it for us”.  But this transparent demand was met with a mysterious, holier-than-thou silence.   Second, for the first time in independent India, we’re using a “double deflator”—ie, using separate measures for input and output inflation rates—to estimate “real” quantities.  Experts: “Sir, congrats on moving to the “double deflator”! Now please give us the mega worksheet of input/output prices and ratios across all industries and operations that you’ve collected to calculate the “double deflator”. That will solve the mystery of why it’s a lowly 2.5 percent while the wholesale and consumer inflation rates are twice, even thrice that number.” State (quixotically): “It’s such a dramatic advancement! Our earlier model of applying consumer or wholesale price inflation to both inputs and output was so blunt, medieval. Because of this scientific change, previous year’s data has been thoroughly revised and cleaned up – yet you do not accept it.” Experts (now irked and irritated): "Sir, we’ve already said it’s a terrific step forward. But don't conflate the demand for reconciling past year’s data with clarity around the “double deflator”. These are two independent streams – two separate enquiries - so don’t try to throw us off-track by mixing them up! The Rs 12 trillion reconciliation must be done on current price data, which is not double deflated.”  State (bigger air of injured innocence): “Why do you need to hark to past practices? Earlier we counted apples, now we are counting oranges. You can’t compare apples and oranges, stop cribbing!”.  Experts (gleam in the eye): “Exactly! If you also give us the current quarter’s GDP on the earlier methodology, we will compare today’s apple with yesterday’s apple. And since you’ve already given us both estimates on the new methodology, we shall compare oranges with oranges. So please just give us the latest GDP print in current prices on the earlier methodology. That’s all we are asking for! C’mon, show the world how transparent and honest our national stats are.” But this innocent, globally benchmarked demand was met with an even more mysterious, holier-than-thou silence.SIR’s 'Illogical Conundrum'—Are We Ek Sau Tees, Or Ek Sau Chalis Cr Hindustanis?The suspicion around EVMs (Electronic Voting Machines) is the other, denser, fog hanging over our transparent democracy. Off the bat, I am not saying that EVMs are being hacked or used to fudge electronic voting. I don’t think there is conclusive evidence to take such a black/white stand. However, equally, there are two potential points of mistrust which are not trivial and need to be seriously addressed.  One, the government claims, sanctimoniously, that an EVM is never attached to the Internet. That’s simply not true. The EVM does link the symbol loading unit (SLU) to the Election Commission’s (EC’s) website–now that’s a connection which could, repeat could, suck in malicious software. The state pleads that only a screenshot is uploaded, not a programmable bug. But why should transparency advocates take the EC at face value? Remember that wise dictum, "Trust, but verify?" Why don’t we open this “junction” of the EVM to the EC’s website to full and continuous scrutiny? Shut the critics up, once and for all? Two, there’s immense scepticism around the way the voting process is wired at the polling booth. When I press the button on the ballot unit, my vote goes to the control unit which instructs the VVPAT (Voter Verified Paper Audit Trail) unit to cut the paper slip and show me the symbol I’ve voted for. Experts fear that when the signal travels back to the control unit, it can be re-programmed, or changed, to get “cast” for a different candidate than the one I voted for and saw on the VVPAT unit. The government contests vehemently but cannot deny that this is a probable chink in the armour.  
So, what’s the fail-safe, unquestionable solution? Simple. Just count all the VVPAT paper slips, and declare the winner on the basis of the paper count if it contradicts the electronic tally. Yes, the results may take an extra 36 hours to be validated, but that’s the tiniest price to pay for scrubbing all cobwebs off the world’s largest democratic elections. Breaking Fake News: India leaps in the Global Transparency Index as she agrees to a full VVPAT count in elections; and publishes raw data for its new GDP estimation methodology! No CCTV, No Accountability, No Problem: EC Scripts Democracy’s Slow Erosion
